subtopic: STATEMENT ON REPORTED DISBANDING OF SERVICE ON BRITISH COLUMBIA COAST

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Marler (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: STATEMENT ON REPORTED DISBANDING OF SERVICE ON BRITISH COLUMBIA COAST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Hahn) inquired last Friday about a press report that the rescue service on the west coast may be disbanded. This report relates to a letter sent by the British Columbia towboat owners' association to my department which, however, reached it only after the report in question had been
published. The letter contains representations as to a small radio station on the second narrows bridge in Vancouver, and raises the question of financial assistance for the work of marine assistance carried out by the association.
I should explain to hon. members that last October a number of proposals regarding marine search and rescue in British Columbia were made to the officials of my department by the association, which operates a most useful volunteer search and rescue organization on the west coast. At that time it was pointed out to the association that some of the matters covered by its proposals did not come under my department, but an assurance was given that the suggestions put forward would be brought to the attention of the proper authorities. This has been done, and the Department of National Defence, which has the responsibility for co-ordinating the actions of the various agencies concerned, has accepted and given effect to some of the proposals made, while others are still under consideration.
Following the discussions with the association last October a number of changes and additions have been made in order to provide improved communication facilities for search and rescue. My department has installed a new multi-channel radio telephone transmitter at the Point Grey coastal radio station operated by it, and this new transmitter is now in service, together with a stand-by transmitter. Though at present the Point Grey station communicates with the rescue co-ordination centre by means of ordinary telephone circuits, the Department of National Defence is setting up a direct telephone circuit to be used exclusively for this purpose and other telephone circuits to enable the rescue co-ordination centre to communicate directly with the ships through our coastal radio station. The present transmitters and the new telephone circuits will, beyond any doubt, provide communication facilities for search and rescue far superior to the limited facility of the radio on the second narrows bridge and other facilities previously available.
To avoid the confusion that would result if several unco-ordinated agencies participated in search and rescue operations, it was decided by the authorities concerned with search and rescue-and not only by my

Inquiries of the Ministry department-that the radio station on the second narrows bridge, which was established for the control of shipping passing the bridge, should, if it intercepted any distress signal, relay it to Point Grey radio station by land telephone, and thereupon the rescue co-ordination centre would exercise its responsibility for search and rescue and communicate with the vessel in distress through the coastal radio station.
So far as the question of financial assistance is concerned, I should like to say that this aspect of the matter is receiving careful consideration, and I hope it will be possible to announce the decision of the government at an early date.
The press report to which the hon. member referred attributed to a representative of the British Columbia towboat owners' association the statement that the fishing boat Zorina had recently sunk because of the decision or order as to the use of the radio station on the second narrows bridge. I am informed that the Zorina did not make use of the international distress frequency reserved exclusively for distress messages which command the help of any ship in a position to afford assistance, although the Point Grey coastal radio station made repeated attempts to communicate with it on that frequency.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed, from Thursday, April 12, consideration of the motion of Hon. W. E. Harris (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in continuing this debate on the budget I should like to state that in my opinion the budget presented to this house on March 20 by the Minister of Finance was one that, in view of present conditions, is responsible and economically sound. It may well be that it was not the budget that many people in Canada would have liked, but I think it is only human and understandable that people look forward to the budget with hopeful expectation that there will be some tax reduction, and that at the same time our economy will continue to boom. Upon reflection, however, I believe there are many people in this land who realize that the budget must not only deal with the wishes of the present but also with the needs of the future. Fancy must not be allowed to outrun wisdom.
I believe, too, that budgetary and monetary policies must be such as to curb inflation and at the same time create that climate which is conducive to our economic growth. Recent budgets have been such as to offer stabilizing controls, while at the same time gradually and effectively reducing taxes, particularly in the personal income tax field. The budget of 1955, described as courageous and optimistic at the time, did what it was designed to do. It gave to our economy the required boost and at the same time enunciated policies that were complementary to the confidence which Canadians have in the future of this country. The present budget is such that many will agree with the approach which it makes to the problems facing those who have the responsibility for their solution.
True it is that our Canadian economy is booming; true it is that people across this land recognize the future possibilities of the development of this country; but I believe, too, they are not unmindful of the many dangers that lurk in the path to progress. More and more money to buy less and less is not an ingredient of prosperity. Inflation can destroy the real aim of prosperity. I am sure that all across this land workers realize that their personal prosperity not only
The Budget-Mr. Batten depends upon the size of their pay envelopes but also upon the capacity of those pay envelopes to provide for themselves and for their families the things that are required.
Plenty is not the product of money; plenty is the product of production, production in an atmosphere of prosperity and stability. I believe that as we look over the size of our national debt, the amount we have to pay for national defence, the cost of our social services, the increased payments for the civil service and the cost of the proposed hospital plan, we could not realistically expect major tax reductions at this time. But while there are no major tax reductions, there are tax reductions of some importance.
I should like to make a comparison between the taxes paid in 1955 by a Canadian whom I shall describe and the taxes paid by him in 1952 under similar conditions. Let us take a married taxpayer with two children and therefore having an apparent exemption of $2,300. If his income in 1952 was $2,500, then his taxable income was $200. In 1952 he paid $35 income tax. In 1955 he paid $28, a reduction of $7, or 20 per cent. If his income were $3,000, his taxable income was $700. In 1952 he paid $123. For the tax year 1955 he paid $98, a reduction of $25, or slightly over 20 per cent. If his income were $3,500 his taxable income would be $1,200. In 1952 he paid $215. For the year 1955 he paid $172, a reduction of $43, or 20 per cent. If his income were $4,000 his taxable income would be $1,700. In 1952 he paid $313. In
1955	he paid $252, a reduction of $61, or again approximately 20 per cent. If his salary were $4,500 his taxable income would be $2,200. In 1952 he paid $417. In 1955 his tax was $336, a reduction of $81, or 19 per cent. If his income were $5,000 his taxable income would be $2,700. In 1952 he paid $529. For the tax year 1955 he has paid, or will pay, $426, a reduction of $103, or again approximately 19 per cent. I submit that in the three years since 1952 personal income taxes have been reduced by approximately 20 per cent. This reduction has been for those in income brackets up to $5,000, which includes over 80 per cent of the taxpayers of Canada.
One asks, "What will happen next year? Will there be a tax reduction?" Yes, of course there will. There will not be a tax reduction due to the rate being lowered, but there will be a tax reduction because the reduction announced last year by the Minister of Finance will be operative for the whole year.
Taking the categories which I have just mentioned, if we were to carry out the calculations we would find that for the tax year
1956	the tax in the first bracket would be

The Budget-Mr. Batten reduced by another $2, making a total reduction since 1952 of 26 per cent. In the $3,000 class the reduction will again be 26 per cent from the year 1952, and so on up to incomes of $5,000. Again I submit that by the end of this year, when taxes will be paid for the tax year 1956, personal income taxes will have been reduced by approximately 25 per cent of the tax paid in the year 1952.
I should now like to make a few remarks with reference to regional development, citing a case from my own riding. There are indeed many factors upon which substantial tax reductions would have to depend, and not the least of these is a continuing rise in our national productivity. In an economy such as ours, efforts to increase our national productivity are left largely to the initiative and drive inherent in the free enterprise system, but at the same time subject to the checks and balances dictated by current conditions. In certain areas conditions are such as to attract private enterprise, and very often there is sufficient economic fertility to sustain and maintain industries which are thriving and prosperous. In other areas the economic climate is not so conducive either to new development or to the expansion of the development already existing, not because the potential is not present but because of changing conditions over which the residents of the area have no control.
May I draw for you a mental picture. Imagine for a moment the west coast of Newfoundland as a line running approximately northeast 300 miles long. Beginning from the southern extremity of this line and going northeast for about 100 miles, there is a parcel of land shaped like an equilateral triangle with its base running due east and west. If the base of this triangle is produced to connect this parcel of land with the mainland of Newfoundland you have what is known in Newfoundland as the Port au Port peninsula.
Years ago this area could have been described as having a farming-fishing economy. During the 1930's the commission government endeavoured to increase the productivity of this area by initiating a scheme of land settlement. In this area, and on the mainland island, there are 30 settlements, including two or three larger settlements and the very progressive town of Stephen-ville. The population of this area totals over 10,000.
Time was when there was a most prosperous scallop industry in Port au Port. This industry was still thriving in the early 1940's, when under the agreement between the United Kingdom and the United States a very large air force base was built on the


outskirts of Stephenville. Over the years the construction program which has been carried on there has provided a large amount of employment for the residents of the area. Since 1949 large draggers have been coming into Port au Port and the scallop beds have been depleted. Today the construction program at Harmon air force base is gradually nearing completion, and there is a fear on the part of some of us that there will be an increase in unemployment in the area.
People feel that there is no reason why there should be unemployment in this area. I believe that with the proper governmental action we could have in the Port au Port area and the offshore limits a greatly improved fishing industry. The proper action would give a boost to the decreasing regional economy and would begin a development which with the present potential would create one of the finest fishing centres on the Atlantic seaboard.
I mention this, first because it is important in my own riding and, second, because I believe in the full development of this land which we call Canada. Sometimes I think of confederation as an experiment in faith. It is an experiment in the faith that people of different racial backgrounds, of different languages, of different creeds, of different physical backgrounds, of different needs and with different problems can by a common aspiration weld unity out of those diversities. I believe the experiment will be successful, but I believe it will be successful only when the development of each area can be raised to that level which is limited only by the extent of the natural resources with which the area has been endowed.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in taking part in the budget debate this afternoon I shall not have very much to say about the budget itself. I make no apology for that, because I have made it a rule which I have tried to follow in this house not to talk, at any rate at any length, about nothing. If I were to be compelled to talk about the budget I would be compelled to break that rule, because never in the history of this parliament since I have been here, and I believe never in the history of the country, have we had a budget so empty, so negative in its approach and so lacking in solutions or even suggestions of solutions for the many pressing problems which confront the Canadian economy.
But I do intend to talk this afternoon about a basic issue, an issue upon which the budget is completely silent, an issue which I believe is the fundamental issue facing Canada today.

It calls for a solution, and it requires government action which would follow from a policy decision which it is imperative to make. I refer to the issue presented by the increasing measure of control and domination of the Canadian economy by United States interests. In no sphere is the government so derelict in its duty to give a lead, to reach a decision and then take the necessary action to remedy the situation as it is in this particular sphere.
The present trend which we see unfolding before us in Canada is a trend which, if allowed to continue, will lead to complete outside domination, certainly of the more important segments of our economy, and probably of all the important segments of our economy. I state as a fact that if this process is allowed to continue, and if it is carried to its logical and ultimate conclusion, the seriousness of the situation will be revealed. History shows us that economic domination, if not resisted, if not altered, inevitably leads by a process of absorption to ultimate political domination as well. So the trend we now see unrolling before us in Canada, as' we analyse the situation, and the lack of action on the part of this government to deal with it, is a trend which evokes the most stringent criticism of the government because it results in developments which work to the detriment of Canadian workmen, which work to the detriment of Canadian business and which in the long run must inevitably work to the detriment of Canadian political integrity itself.
I intend in the course of my remarks, if time permits, to suggest some measures which can and should be taken-measures, it is true, which would involve some difficulty, but all these important matters involve the making of difficult but essential decisions. I do not for a moment suggest that the decisions and the implementation of the policy behind those decisions will not be beset with some difficulties. but I do intend now or on another occasion to suggest some measures which can and should be taken to remedy the situation and to halt the trend that we see developing before our eyes.
Before coming to the main subject of my remarks this afternoon I should like to suggest that this matter should be examined in the light of the background which is presented today. There are two particular features of that background that I intend to mention. The first is the background presented by the speech made in Vancouver yesterday by the retiring United States ambassador, Mr. Douglas Stuart, and the second is the picture painted by a booklet released
The Budget-Mr. Fulton at the beginning of this month by the dominion bureau of statistics, entitled "Canada's International Investment Position, 1926 to 1954."
To deal first with the extraordinary and unprecedented statement made yesterday by the United States ambassador, Mr. Stuart, I would say that it seems to me that his speech and the implications of that speech present in the clearest possible light a measure of the seriousness of the situation we now face. We have here an unprecedented example of conduct on the part of a man whom we have always regarded as a responsible and friendly man, a man who has had many friendly relations with Canadians at all levels, governmental, political, business and in the sphere of the general community. The fact that this responsible and friendly man, this ambassador of a friendly country, would intervene directly in an issue which is now being discussed as a domestic issue in Canada, is itself a measure of the seriousness of the situation. That he would regard it as his right and his duty to do so shows how far things have gone along the line of acceptance of American domination, and how far the relationship between our two countries has progressed that it would lead this man to believe that he had the right to intervene in domestic affairs in Canada in this way.
I was and am amazed that he could do so. I am extremely disturbed that he should do so. I am reluctant, I am almost unwilling, to believe that matters have got to the point between our two governments that it would have been suggested to him by his own government that he should thus intervene. I find it, therefore, extremely difficult to believe that his remarks were inspired from Washington, and that leaves me with the assumption, of necessity, that his remarks must have been inspired from Ottawa. This conclusion is the more compelling because we have this situation; that with a domestic controversy going on here, a fundamental difference of political opinion between the government and the opposition, a matter obviously reserved to discussion and decision here in parliament, we have the United States ambassador going to Vancouver expressing exactly the sort of criticism which the government is expressing, in an attempt to becloud the issue and misrepresent the stand the official opposition is taking. It seems to me that this must be regarded as the action of a government here in Ottawa which has so debauched Canadian politics that it uses the United States ambassador as a tool to advance its own political interests.

His master's voice. Do I understand that the hon. gentlemen opposite accept the suggestion that they have inspired these remarks? He goes on:
"-it is being discussed emotionally perhaps more than logically, it is one for which some of those who raise it do not appear to be seeking a solution but rather the creation of an issue."
That, of course, is exactly the attitude of the government, which refuses, in keeping with the traditional Liberal attitude, to see any issue involved in the domination of the Canadian economy by United States interests. It has got to the point that the United States ambassador, the emissary from the government at Washington, says he finds it extraordinary that Canadians should be concerned over the extent to which this development has been taking place. He finds it extraordinary that Canadians should be concerned when they awake to the realization that nearly 50 per cent of their manufacturing industry is under the control of United States interests, that over 50 per cent of their mining industry is under the control of United States capital, and that nearly 70 per cent of their petroleum industry is under the control of United States capital. He finds it extraordinary that we


should be concerned about these developments. The article continues:
Mr. Stuart suggested that some of the phrases and questions emanating from those critical of U.S. investment in Canada are being used deliberately to create a maximum of suspicion and rasp the pride and self-respect of any Canadian-and risk, for sometimes selfish motives, the raising of a barrier between the two countries.
The Globe and Mail article reporting his speech goes on to say:
Recalling a recent speech by a person he described as a prominent Canadian, Mr. Stuart said, "This speaker had warned, in a somewhat emotional appeal, that we are not going to be treated as though we were the 50th state of the United States ... We are not going to be hewers of wood, drawers of water, and diggers of holes for any other country, no matter how friendly that country may be."
In the same speech, Mr. Stuart continued, the speaker readily conceded that investment from the United States and elsewhere has been largely responsible for the pace of Canadian expansion within these past few years.
We have no quarrel with Mr. Stuart that Canada is dependent in large degree upon outside capital for help in the development of our resources. We and the prominent Canadian to whom it is apparent that Mr. Stuart was referring, and whom we know and respect as the Leader of the Opposition, have always recognized that it is essential to have outside capital to help in the development of our resources and have in fact taken positive steps to encourage and support that trend. But the fundamental difference between ourselves and the government and apparently the fundamental difference between ourselves and Mr. Stuart is that we say that the processing must take place under Canadian control, Canadian regulation and in the interests of the Canadian economy and development rather than that of the United States.
There, of course, there is a fundamental difference; and there, of course, we are entitled to say that when a United States ambassador states that he finds it extraordinary and believes there should be no concern on the part of Canadians that in fact our resources have passed from under our own control he is, of course, illustrating the seriousness of the situation and demonstrating positively that this is the feeling of his government and of the government here, which does not quarrel with his statements and is espousing a policy which is diametrically opposed to the best interests of Canada.
Since the speech of this gentleman has raised, by its direct intervention in the discussion of Canadian domestic affairs, the question of the attitude and position of this party, let me say at once in order to set the record straight that never has our leader

or the party which he leads suggested at any time that anything should be done in Canada to discourage the investment of United States or any other capital in Canada to assist us in the development of our resources. In fact we have encouraged it and say it should be encouraged. We say that as the result of such investment they should share in the benefits and advantages we will receive but that the direction, policy, control and a share of the advantages should be reserved for the benefit of Canada.
I have but to remind the house and you, sir, of the record of my leader in this regard when he was premier of Ontario and when, as a result of the actions he took as premier, he was successful in having invested in Ontario some quarter of a billion dollars of United States capital to the advantage of the economy of that province, particularly in the northern and hitherto undeveloped areas, and was almost exclusively responsible for the tremendous development in the pulp and paper industry, the erection of those huge plants in northern Ontario under Canadian direction and regulation, contributing advantages and benefits to the Canadian economy which were shared by the Americans on terms which the Americans were glad and happy to accept.
That is the policy which we adopt here. I should like to read into the record a press release issued today by the leader of this party, in order to contrast the policy of our leader as I have outlined it and as set forth in this press release with the sort of statements Mr. Stuart and his government have been making. This is a press release issued today, April 17, by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew), and it reads as follows:
It is unfortunate indeed that Mr. Stuart, whom we had all regarded so highly as such an understanding friend of Canada, should have chosen to give as his farewell message so inaccurate an interpretation of Canadian sentiment toward investors from the United States. So far as I am aware, no responsible Canadian has suggested that we do not welcome such investment. Many have urged, however, and will continue to urge, that the Canadian government take appropriate steps to encourage Canadian industry to process a larger proportion of our raw materials for the employment of a greater number of Canadians here in Canada. That is something very different from the interpretation given to quotations which have been removed from their context and their meaning.
I should also like to set alongside that, as a proper statement of the attitude which should prevail in Canada and in contrast with the sentiments expressed by the United States ambassador, some extracts from an editorial which appeared in the April 14 issue of Business Week, one of the most influential of United States magazines. This editorial establishes clearly that thoughtful Americans
The Budget-Mr. Fulton and thoughtful American industrialists recognize that Canada has justifiable cause to be concerned about the trend which is now taking place, of the passage of control of substantial segments of the Canadian economy directly into the hands of United States interests. The editorial has this to say:
When two nations are so deeply involved in each other's economic and political destinies, and when one of the two is larger and wealthier than the other, occasions for conflict will never be lacking. At present, Canada has a long list of concerns about the United States, including:
Heavy United States investment in and control over a significant portion of Canada's oil, mining and manufacturing industries. Fear that United States interests may gain control of the proposed trans-Canada gas pipe line is a particular irritant.
United States tariff and customs policies, which Canadians feel discriminate against their processed and manufactured goods and which worsen Canada's chronic imbalance in her trade with us.
The United States way of disposing of surplus farm commodities . . .
Then I am omitting some words.
The enormous flow to Canada of United States consumer goods, movies and publications . . .
United States unwillingness to be limited by provisions of a 1909 treaty in the dispute with Canada over access to hydro power on the Columbia river. Canadians say we accepted these provisions so long as they worked in our favour but now want to ignore them when they seem to give Canada an advantage.
I express the hope that in the forthcoming negotiations forecast by the Prime Minister, Canada will do nothing to retreat from or to sabotage the position adopted on behalf of this country under which we stand firm on article 2 of that treaty which now works to our advantage and without which we would be unable to develop the tremendous potential hydro resource of the Columbia river. Then the editorial goes on to say:
We don't expect those Canadian grievances that have a real basis to evaporate. Nor do we deny Canada the right to regulate its own affairs, even when we doubt the wisdom of the methods it chooses.
Finally they say:
We won't attempt here to judge the merits of the specific Canadian grievances against us. All we want to emphasize now is our hope that the grievances will stay specific, will not degenerate into that emotion which could more properly be called "anti-American". We both have too much at stake in our partnership to endanger it by a general and irrational hostility.
With that last sentiment we here in this party in the official opposition thoroughly agree. We have specific causes for concern, and it is those specific matters which we wish to discuss and upon which we wish to see the government take specific action. Instead of washing their linen over the back fence by speeches made by the minister in Chicago and in other places which can have
2998	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Fulton no good purpose, we wish to see these problems resolved by specific decisions by the Canadian government within our own jurisdiction and proper to our own political integrity and independence. We wish to see action taken so the development of Canada can remain under Canadian control and be carried on in the interests of Canada generally. I therefore ask you, Mr. Speaker, to contrast that responsible and thoughtful editorial, which was a proper statement of the position, with the complete and deliberate misrepresentation-I must unfortunately describe it as that-made by the retiring United States ambassador.
I suggest there should also be a contrast between the timorous attitude of this government-that you cannot take any measures that will insist on Canadian regulation, direction and control of our resources because it may hurt or offend United States investors- with the attitude of responsible American commentators and businessmen who say they would be willing to accept proper Canadian policies and actions designed to preserve the integrity of the Canadian economy and to ensure that it would be under Canadian direction, and that they would be willing to invest in Canada subject to those conditions. All I can say there is that the timorous attitude of this government and its refusal to take the necessary action contrasts ill with the realistic and friendly approach of responsible American businessmen themselves.
I should now like to turn to the second feature of the background of the situation as contained in the dominion bureau of statistics release. It is going to be necessary for me to place several quotations on record from their introductory comments, which are based upon the statistical tables which they have themselves compiled. This is the result of a survey of Canada's international investment position from the year 1926 to the year 1954. On page 9 they say this:
Non-resident ownership of Canadian manufacturing now amounts to about a half of the total capital employed and to well over a half in the case of mining, smelting and petroleum. These proportions of ownership have risen rapidly since 1948 as shown in statement 18. Likewise the proportions of these Canadian industries which are controlled abroad have been increasing even more as shown in statement 19.
Then they point out that there is a significant change in the trend, and that while it is true that in the over-all picture Canadian investment now represents a larger proportion of the total capital invested in Canada than was the case in the past, Canadian investment in what they describe as the dynamic field of development is in fact shrinking whereas the Canadian investment that is increasing is in


the more static fields of residential property and related fields. They say:
The nature and distribution of Canadian savings and the opportunities open for individual and public investment have had the effect of concentrating much of Canadian investment in less dynamic forms than some of the investments by non-resident concerns . . .
Then again on page 10 we find this:
A highly significant aspect of the rapidly increasing foreign investments in Canada is their concentration in direct investments in Canadian industry which carry with them control and ownership of equities in areas of Canadian mining and industrial production undergoing accelerated Canadian development. In the field of industry which includes manufacturing, mining and petroleum nonresident controlled companies represent more than half of the estimated total capital invested. In manufacturing alone excluding petroleum refining, the non-resident controlled portion in 1953 was some 47 per cent, and in petroleum 70 per cent, and in other mining 55 per cent.
Let me emphasize the words "non-resident controlled." Finally they say this:
Most of these concerns were controlled in the United States.
Again on page 13 they say:
And the form has also changed, more now being for direct investment in economic development while less represents investment in new issues of bonds than in the 1920's.
There they are again emphasizing the fact that the form of American investment is now in equity capital giving direct control rather than in the borrowed capital which would be more by way of pure assistance. Then at page 25 they give the number of foreign-controlled concerns, which in 1954 amounted to 3,361. Finally I would direct attention particularly to the table found at page 84 which shows that in 1953 less than one-third of the petroleum companies operating in Canada were controlled in Canada and that more than two-thirds were controlled in the United States.
That is the background, and it establishes two things; first, things have got to the point that the American ambassador thinks it proper to intervene in Canadian domestic issues, and finds it extraordinary that Canadians should be concerned over the extent of American control; second, the figures contained in this bureau of statistics survey which show that in manufacturing, mining and petroleum, which are the three areas of most rapid development in Canada, from one-half to two-thirds is now under American control. It is with that background that we must assess the situation and on the basis of which we charge the government with most serious dereliction of 'duty.
Mr. Speaker, it is perhaps not surprising that the government should be open to this charge because, after all, they are but continuing in the present the pattern which they

have followed over many years. Let us look at that pattern for a moment. I should like to spend rather more time than I have at my disposal in tracing the pattern of American thought and their attitude toward this problem, not on the basis of hostility to them but because I believe it is essential to take a calm and dispassionate look at the trends which are revealed by the developments of history.
It is a fact that the Americans have, by and large over the years, almost unconsciously adopted the attitude that the North American continent belongs to them. They are friendly with us; they want to see us co-operate, but always in the back of their minds has been the thought-and I believe it is still there- that by some sort of predestination they are ordained to be the controlling factor forever. That is not just by virtue of their position south of the 49th parallel, but by extension of their influence, directly and indirectly, north of the 49th parallel. They believe that they are to control the North American continent.
We have seen in the past the attempts they have made to control Canada. There were military attempts starting back with the raiding parties in the days of the American revolution. Then there was the war of 1812, when they made an attempt at military conquest. There were the Fenian raids of the 1850's and 1860's. Then having abandoned military attempts, they undertook political attempts. We from the west remember the slogan "54-40 or fight". Had it not been for those who believed in the preservation of a Canadian nation north of the 49th parallel, British Columbia as it now exists and parts of the other provinces would be part of the United States.
Then there followed exertions and activities in the economic sphere. There were attempts looking toward commercial union in the 1880's. There was the attempt by blackmail to acquire control of the Canadian Pacific Railway. One has only to read that chapter of Creighton's recent biography of Sir John A. Macdonald to appreciate that the Americans, knowing a good thing when they saw one, were attempting to gain control of the Canadian Pacific Railway and resorted even to blackmail in an attempt to do it. In spite of the efforts by the party of which my hon. friends opposite are the successors to hand over the control of that great enterprise to the United States, it was Sir John A. Macdonald and his dedication to the idea of a Canadian nation that was successful eventually in resisting these economic attempts, which even resorted to blackmail.
The Budget-Mr. Fulton
There are some interesting bits of history in this connection. I should like to place before the house some quotations which one finds in a very excellent book compiled by Mr. Hamilton of our own library staff, entitled "Canadian Quotations and Phrases". On page 3 of that book one finds the following quotation:
AH Americans are unfortunately possessed with a vague notion that Canada is somehow or other to fall into their hands without a war.
These words were spoken by Henry S. Fox, the British minister to Washington in November, 1838.
Coming a little more up to date, on page 4 we find this:
Nobody who has studied the peculiar methods by which elections are won in Canada-
I ask my hon. friends opposite to consider this and its implications.
-will deny the fact that five or six million dollars, judiciously expended .	.	. would secure the
return to parliament of a majority pledged to the annexation of Canada to the United States.
This quotation was taken from the New York World of 1890.
On the same page we find this quotation:
I am for it (the Reciprocity agreement) because I hope to see the day when the American flag will float over every square foot of the British North American possessions clear to the north pole.
This statement was made by Champ Clark, Speaker of the House of Representatives in Washington in 1911.
It is not strange, Mr. Speaker, that the Liberal party here which contemplated commercial union in the 1880's and reciprocity in 1911 should now view with equanimity the process in 1956 whereby the United States will take us over through economic control, without having to traverse any obstacles whatever. That is the danger, unless the trend is checked and reversed, which requires a fundamental decision and positive government action.
One might come a bit closer to home, to our own political history, and refer to a quotation from Sir Wilfrid Laurier found on page 25 of this book as an indication of the attitude of the party opposite. Remember this was in the context of 1891, when we had not yet developed a full sense of Canadian nationality. This is the quotation:
I am a subject of the British crown, but whenever I have to choose between the interests of England and Canada it is manifest to me that the interests of my country are identical with those of the United States of America.
This was from a speech by Sir Wilfrid Laurier delivered in Boston in 1891. Here is a final quotation from Sir Wilfrid, found on page 230:
We are living beside a great neighbour who. I believe I can say without being deemed unfriendly

The Budget-Mr. Fulton to them, are very grasping in their national acts, and who are determined upon every occasion to get the best in any agreement which they make.
That is looking back into history and that is the attitude honestly and conscientiously adopted by my hon. friends opposite, and it is the policy which we see revealed today in their attempts to discredit those who say that the Canadian government must make the simple fundamental decision which will have the result that control of the Canadian economy and the direction of Canadian development is going to remain in Canadian hands.
There are many other contrasts which I should like to draw between the attitude of the government as we see it now, as it unfolds before our eyes, and the attitude which should be adopted. As one of the most outstanding events, I should like to refer to the historical position of this party as revealed in connection with the Canadian Pacific Railway. During the 1870's and 1880's when this country was faced with the superhuman task of building a railway to unite Canada and start a nation north of the 49th parallel, there was only one place to go to get the capital. We did go to the foreign capital markets of London and, to a lesser extent, New York. Today we recognize, as I have said, that for Canadian development to take place at the pace we would like to see it take place, we must invite and welcome outside capital. But in those days the Canadian government did not hesitate to say, "You may come in; you are welcome and you can share in the advantages and benefits, but you will remain under Canadian control."
I have referred to the attempt, even going so far as blackmail, by the United States to get control of the Canadian Pacific, which we resisted. In 1881 when the statute incorporating the Canadian Pacific Railway was passed there was written into that statute a provision that the majority of the directors, of whom the president shall be one, shall be British subjects. Bearing in mind the historical and political realities of that day, there being no such thing as a Canadian citizen, that was equivalent to saying that the majority should be Canadian and the majority of the directors of the Canadian Pacific Railway have been and are to this day Canadian. As a result of that simple decision made in 1881 the policy, control and direction of that company remains responsive to and primarily concerned with, the interests of Canada and not any foreign country. This government refuses steadfastly, stubbornly, narrowly and unimaginatively to take such simple measures.
There is, I think, another matter which should be borne in mind. We look at things

that have happened in other countries, and we sometimes offhandedly dismiss countries such as Mexico and the Argentine as being somewhat less stable than our own. But remember these countries woke up one day to realize that the control of vital segments of their economy had passed entirely into foreign hands. They were left with two simple alternatives; one, to accept the inevitable consequence which would be eventual political domination as well by outside interests; the other, to take some action to deal with it. What action was left open to them? There was only the extreme, violent and nationalistic action of expropriation.
We all remember when Mexico expropriated the tremendous oil industry, which at that time was virtually a United States monopoly in that country. We must take thought of these matters in Canada. We must not allow the situation to develop to the point where we wake up suddenly one day to find that is the only recourse that is left open to us, either political annexation as the inevitable consequence or some drastic, violent action which we would not like to contemplate upon sober reflection.

The general public is perhaps not always aware that, each year, the government pays out millions to the hospitals of the various provinces.
This is probably due to the fact that these grants are not surrounded by election talk, as it is done in other quarters. The federal government is decent enough not to have any underlying political motives when it is granting those subsidies. There are no strings attached to these grants with regard to the choice of such and such contractor, architect or engineer, a practice to which we have become accustomed in a certain province. I think the government is to be commended in this respect.
Unfortunately, some people are seen to take advantage from a moderation that is all to the government's credit, creating the general impression that the construction of these hospitals or the enlargement of existing facilities is entirely due to them.
It is therefore to be hoped that this discretion on the part of the government is not such as to help his opponents and does not become a political argument that they could use against it.
I was very pleased to see the government provide a pension for the disabled. I am convinced that, in this field, this is just a beginning and that the legislation setting up this pension will be gradually improved so as to increase the number of disabled people who can take advantage of it.
I am happy also to notice that bilingualism is making substantial progress in this house as well as in this country as a whole. We must however work relentlessly to make bilingualism a general practice in this country. Much is left to be done. National unity, however, can only be achieved on such a basis.
Until the time when every member in this house is able to use both languages with equal ease, I suggest that it is necessary for everyone to have a full understanding of parliamentary debates and for that purpose a simultaneous translation system should be established as soon as possible.
In December 1952 I had expressed the wish that this system be established. I hope that before too long the necessary equipment will be installed in the house.
We have just finished discussing the budget.
I wish to avail myself of this opportunity to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) for having managed to balance his budget in spite of the ever increasing demands facing the government.
In the field of taxation, I hope that the last plan submitted to the provinces will ultimately result in some tax relief. At least
17, 1956
The Budget-Mr. Lefrangois indirectly. A few years ago, the government of one province introduced a provincial tax which, according to its allegations, was supposed to bring in $25 million a year. It was said then, to justify that new provincial tax, that the province did not get its share of revenue.
Under the new plan that province, without signing any agreement, will receive almost twice the amount she anticipated from the provincial tax. It would therefore be in order to drop that provincial tax and thus relieve the population of that province from that burden.
As far as the federal income tax is concerned, I hope that a deduction of 5 per cent of the taxable income will soon be allowed, without the necessity of producing a receipt for gifts to charitable institutions.
I believe indeed that, as a general rule, few people in this country, as taxpayers, contribute less than 5 per cent of their income to charity.
I do not mean thereby to deny to those who donate more, the provisions of the act as it now stands, allowing deductions up to 10 per cent of the taxable income on production of receipts. In other words, I hope the act will authorize all taxpayers to deduct automatically 5 per cent of their taxable income without receipts. If, on the other hand, taxpayers who contribute more wish to deduct the full amount of their donations up to 10 per cent of their taxable income, they should be able to continue to do so, provided however that they submit receipts for the full amount of their deductions with their return.
I believe that system would be fair to all and would spare, to income tax services as well as to those who have to issue receipts, the great complications involved in the present system.
Mr. Speaker, may I be allowed, in conclusion, to express the respect and admiration of my constituents for the members of the cabinet, this magnificent team which, under a true leader, the right hon. Prime Minister, presides with such obvious success over the destinies of our country.
The development this country is undergoing at the present time is without precedent in its history. Never before have Canadians enjoyed such a high standard of living, never before has this country been more powerful nor more respected and esteemed.
The more we move through the chapters of the history being written at this time the more grand and glorious becomes the title

The Budget-Mr. Castleden of Canadian. Every day brings new reasons to boast of this title and to feel how good it is to live in a wonderful country such as qurs.
So let us stop sometimes and think that these last pages of history have been written at the dictation of our present Prime Minister, the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my intention this afternoon to deal with two aspects of the present situation in Canada with regard to our budget, and to mention the things that are in a very real way affecting, not only the Canadian people of today very greatly but will have, I believe, an even greater effect on the Canada of tomorrow.
The budget which was brought down in the house a few weeks ago showed that we were continuing to tax the Canadian people to the extent of about $4 billion a year on an increased national gross product, and that we intend to expend under that budget almost $2 billion for national defence.
The members of the House of Commons have termed this budget a "do nothing" budget and I think rightly so, because the serious defects of the budget of a year ago have not been rectified in this one, and the same glaring shortcomings in Canada's part in the international picture and in the pursuit of peace in the world are not being made effective. I refer to the fact that Canada expends almost $2 billion, or almost half her total tax revenue, on national defence, on guided missiles, jet planes and the most modern weapons of warfare. In its effort to promote peace in the western world Canada provides a miserable pittance of about $30 million for such things as the Colombo plan and economic aid. This country spends almost $1,700 million on national defence and only one-sixtieth of that amount on economic aid. Under such circumstances Canada is not pulling her weight or doing her part in trying to establish peace in the world.
Here is a Canada overburdened with surpluses, unable to use our potential production to provide the things the world needs so much and which could be used to such great advantage in bringing peace to the world, in helping backward areas of the world and feeding nations which are hungry, nations which tomorrow will decide whether the western world and western ideas of democracy shall succeed. The government


says nothing about this in the budget; therefore I submit it can properly be termed a do-nothing budget.
Surely our attitude toward the world situation should not be so pagan and outworn as to believe that we are going to conquer the world or win it to our way of life, with a show of strength or of apparent superiority; that fear is going to cause these people to look up to us and say that democracy as exemplified by the west is the best for the world.
Is there a country with a greater potential for helping the world toward democracy? We could not only help the world abroad, we could help our own economy. We could help to balance our own Canadian economy and provide some economic security to those people in our midst who are trying to do their bit by producing food, grain, meat and other things which the world needs so badly. Here is this government with one of the largest surpluses we have ever had. The Minister of Finance boasts about the great surplus that he has provided for Canada at this time.

Of course the budget is a do-nothing budget. It is a do-nothing budget because it has done nothing about taxing the kind of capital gains which attract these people here to take Canada's resources and assume control of our interests. What is the future of Canada with this kind of policy? It is time for every Canadian who believes in Canada for Canadians to make his voice heard in protest.
This issue is of the greatest importance. It is the culmination of what threatened the Canadian people in 1911 when they threw out reciprocity and said they wanted Canada to be developed for the Canadian people. Now, without even an election, the government, making use of the majority given the Liberal party in 1953, is carrying out the very thing which the people do not want. I maintain the people of Canada do not want it in 1956. They just do not realize what is going on in Canada. They are told that everything is fine.
I think what is happening in Canada today should be made known to all the people of Canada. In recent months I have talked to people from the east and west of Canada, and I have been astounded at the lack of even an elementary understanding or knowledge of what is happening even with respect to the trans-Canada pipe line. When people find out they are astounded and awakened. Unfortunately information is not reaching the public as it should.
I maintain that the people of Canada should be made aware of the situation. I appeal to those members sitting on the government side to search their hearts and souls very deeply, because they are responsible for what is happening in Canada today. If, knowing what is happening, they remain silent and say nothing, if they fail to raise their voices, they will be derelict in their duties and future generations will condemn them. subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my contribution to this debate will be limited to a few minutes.
Last year I voted in favour of the government budget proposals. I considered then that the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) had at least made a step in the right direction and I felt that we were bound to show him our appreciation.
This year I will have to vote against the budget, as I feel that the hon. minister has made no further progress in the direction which he took last year.
For instance, as far as the income tax is concerned, it seems to me that the basic

exemption should have been raised to $2,000 or at least to $1,500 for unmarried people, and to $3,000 for heads of families.
Moreover, the 8 per cent sales tax should have been reduced and family allowances should have been readjusted so as to raise their real purchasing power to its level of ten or eleven years ago.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They will do that next year, just before the election.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
You have to admit that these three suggestions are made with a view to giving a special protection to family heads, and more particularly to the heads of large families.
Even with a rate increase of 50 or 60 per cent, family allowances would cover but a small fraction of what it costs to support a child. If you add to that the 8 per cent sales tax, the cost of which is multiplied by the number of consumers in the household, you have to conclude that in our modern society it has become a luxury to have a large family and to maintain a decent home where it is good to live. Indeed, it is absolutely necessary that the home be so organized that it will appeal to the child. Such being the case he will be in a position to receive an education and upbringing which he would be unable to find anywhere else.
It does seem to me, though, that the head of the family cannot organize such a home if his salary, which is no more than adequate at the present time, is further reduced by the encroachments of an overly burdensome tax system.
It should not be necessary to insist once more upon the fact that the greatest of modern sociologists, whatever their race, religion or country, continue to state that the family is the basic element of society and that the latter will be what the former will make it. However, families, like individuals, must enjoy that modicum of well-being necessary to the full flowering of moral and spiritual values.
That is why I urge the Minister of Finance, if he is unwilling to change his present budget, at least to see to it that next year's brings about the changes I have just indicated.
I wish to add a few words in conclusion with regard to the pension paid to disabled people.	.
I may be wrong but it seems to me that any person exercising a trade or occupation who, following sickness or accident, can no longer fulfil permanently the position formerly occupied in this same trade, or a closely related position, any such person should be considered as a disabled person.

As regards those who, from birth or from early age, were never able, because of mental or physical deficiency, to integrate themselves in a class of employment allowing them to earn a major part of their living expenses, they should also be considered as disabled persons.
It matters little whether or not these people can dress and walk by themselves, as stated in the application forms, whether or not they are capable of climbing stairs without difficulty, that is secondary.
Besides, at the rate of things, with modern progress in material things and the setback of morals, the day is not far away when there will be no more stairs to climb or when we shall no longer have to dress as, having shown all that there is to show, we shall have nothing left to conceal. Nevertheless we will still have to work in order to earn a living, and this is the only thing-I mean on a material basis-which seems essential to me. When such a possibility exists no longer, and when there is no other source of income to compensate for work, then I feel that the government ought to step in.
I am far from asserting, however, that the hon. Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), and the provincial ministers co-operating with him, have grasped nothing of the problem; quite the contrary.
From the meetings of experts representing both sides, since the act has been in force, a substantial improvement has resulted in so far as the understanding of the problem and the means of solving it are concerned. However, we must go farther. It would be better perhaps to give less importance to the wording of the regulation forms and leave the experts -in the case the examining doctors-with more freedom in the way they may establish, for all practical purposes, the degree of disability of any particular individual.
I trust however that within a few years we will have a disabled persons pension act such as to meet the needs of our people. I quite understand that this cannot be achieved at the first strike; that is why I ask the hon. Minister of National Health and Welfare to keep on doing his best, in co-operation with the various provincial authorities who seem to me equally well disposed, in order to improve this legislation the principle of which is excellent, but the working of which is still not perfect.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have now reached the concluding day of the budget debate. In spite of the
The Budget-Mr. Patterson many criticisms that have been voiced and the inadequacies that have been outlined it is possible that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) is still of the opinion that he brought down a satisfactory budget. If he will not be convinced of the contrary, perhaps he could at least find standing room halfway between the criticisms of the amendment which refers to it as empty, negative and partisan and, on the other hand, the laudatory remarks of the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Robertson) when he stated that the budget was realistic, responsible and encouraging. I would suggest that even there the minister might find the ground rather shaky. Perhaps it could be said, however, that within the inadequate framework of the present monetary and fiscal policies of the government he is doing a fair job. Nevertheless, having regard to the possibilities were the government to adopt policies suitable to the age in which we live, the accomplishments are far from being satisfactory.
Not only in Canada, Mr. Speaker, but in other countries of the commonwealth and of the world sincere men are beginning to realize that something must be done if all the people are to be assured of a share in the country's production and are to maintain and enjoy the standard of living possible in an age of plenty. I am sure that hon. members will be aware of the fact that in New Zealand a royal commission on banking, credit and currency was set up last year to study the entire matter of monetary reform. Since that time the hearings have been brought to a conclusion. I have in my hand a booklet entitled, "Royal Commission on Banking, Credit and Currency." The monetary royal commission commenced the hearing of evidence in Wellington on April 28 and concluded on September 30, 1955.
This booklet is made up of excerpts from the official verbatim report and reprints from the Mirror published in Auckland, New Zealand. On page 10 of this particular booklet we have a reference to the review of evidence. I might say that this is published by the editor of the Mirror, Mr. H. J. Kelliher. In this review of evidence we read this statement:
There has been a substantial measure of agreement between the people who have appeared before the commission as critics of the present banking procedure. On the main and basic issues, the federation of labour, the social credit association and Mr. Kelliher form a united front. They contend-(1) that the banks do not lend their deposits: (2) that the banks create monetary credit and charge interest on this created money; (3) that all moneys should be issued by the state in accordance with its sovereign prerogative; (4) that the booms and slumps which New Zealand has experienced and which have been a feature of British economic history during the past century
3008	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Patterson
have been accentuated by the expansion and contraction of bank credit; (5) that as a first step towards economic stability the banks must be deprived'of the power to create and destroy money which they should never have been allowed to exercise.
I just give that to call to the attention of members of the house that the federation of labour, the social credit association and Mr. Kelliher all agree on these basic and fundamental points.
In a covering letter that was sent out with this booklet, Mr. Kelliher states:
Democracy's greatest need today is a monetary system under which neither booms nor slumps will recur, and inflation will not again break through and steal the earnings and savings of the people. It is the sovereign duty of every government to issue money and regulate its value-ensuring at all times an adequate but not excessive money supply. Thus the purchasing power of the people's earnings and savings will be safeguarded.
We have also information indicating that in the United Kingdom there is a realization on the part of a great many people that something is radically wrong with the present monetary situation. Representations have been made to Mr. Harold Macmillan, chancellor of the exchequer, and he apparently agreed to meet with a delegation of those who were concerned about this matter.
I again refer to the royal commission on banking, credit and currency set up in New Zealand. There is another section which is called, "The Case for Social Crediters". Let me emphasize again that the man who makes this statement is not a social crediter. He does differ from Social Credit in some particular respects. On page 18 we read these words:
I don't know whether the commission reached, or can reach, any conclusion after its many days of probing into the Social Credit ideals of Mr. Young and the gracious educated lady from Dunedin. But I doubt if any conclusion could be reached other than that Social Credit correctly diagnoses the cause of our present troubles, but the main proposals for its remedy are somewhat nebulous.
I give that to call attention to the fact that he agrees Social Credit has pinpointed the problem and diagnosed the situation, pointed out the weaknesses of the present system. With reference to the royal commission currently sitting on Canada's economic prospects, we regret that there is nothing in the terms of reference authorizing that commission to study proposals for monetary reform. The commission can look into the prospects and consider all these other angles, yet their terms of reference do not include the study of monetary reform proposals. We in the Social Credit movement consider that such investigations are of the utmost importance. When we consider the whole financial picture of Canada, consider our taxation


structure, the tremendous volume of our national debt and the cost of financing that national debt, then certainly we say that something should be done to face this matter realistically and bring some alterations that would put us on a more substantial and more favourable financial foundation.
However, Mr. Speaker, we are still struggling along under the old, outmoded financial system and therefore we must consider the budget, I suppose, in the light of that fact. I want to refer to a number of matters which come very close to the people of Canada. First of all, I should like to say how disappointed we are to find that in the budget presentation, and considering the matters that the government is introducing at this session, no mention is made of the position in which our senior citizens still find themselves. I recall referring to this particular matter in the budget debate last year and pointing out the serious situation that our senior citizens are facing. I joined with many other members in the house in requesting that something be done to alleviate their difficult situation and bring some increase in their pensions and in their allowances. I read the reply that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) gave to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) as recorded, I believe, on page 184 of Hansard for January 17, 1956, and I felt at that time that his response was very inadequate and certainly did not indicate the concern he should have felt for the people in this particular category. I would say that his argument was very inconclusive because no one can question the fact that our senior citizens are in a desperate plight at the present time.
We do not have to labour that point because I am sure that when one considers the allowance that the senior citizens are receiving one will fully realize that in no way is it adequate to meet the cost of living at the present time. They are just barely getting by and stretching the very last cent to the maximum. But a great many of them are finding that before the next cheque comes in there are several days during which they have nothing with which to purchase food and carry them through until the cheque arrives. It is not as if Canada was not in a position to do something further in this regard. When we think of the expenditures, when we think of the wealth of Canada, when we think of all these things, then there is absolutely no reason why we could not give some added assistance to our senior citizens to make life a little easier for them, a little more comfortable, and show them that we are at least thinking about them and are concerned about their welfare. When we think of their contribution to Canada, in service,

in sacrifice and in money, let me say that these people deserve a better deal than they are getting from the federal government.
Let me refer to a resolution which was passed at the second annual convention of the Marpole community centre in Vancouver in June of last year. In article 11 the senior citizens' association of British Columbia said:
Whereas Canada was one of the most enthusiastic advocates of the universal declaration of human rights passed by the United Nations: and
Whereas this declaration guarantees freedom from want to people residing in nations signing the declaration; and
Whereas hundreds of thousands of pensioners in Canada are trying to live on a totally inadequate pension and are in want of the sheer necessities of life;
Now therefore be it resolved that this convention of senior citizens' association of British Columbia calls on the government of Canada to implement its own signature to the declaration of human rights by providing a pension sufficient to ensure that pensioners are not in want.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I would like to add my voice to the pleas of other hon. members in asking that the pensions of our senior citizens be raised, or at least their value be restored to the level enjoyed when those pensions and this system were first instituted. I should also like to again request that the senior citizens' pensions be paid regardless of where the pensioners may choose to spend their declining days. I have received a letter dated January 9, 1956, from a resident of Vancouver. The letter reads as follows:
Dear Sir:
Being a member of the federal house of parliament, could I ask a favour of you concerning the old age pension?
I am receiving the $40 a month pension and my relations in England have asked me to finish my days with them.
I have lived in British Columbia since 1908 and have no relations or ties in this country, and would like to go to England. But I do not wish to be a burden on them if my savings run out.
Is there any way that I can have the pension transferred to England?
I am informed I can leave the country for six months and on return get three months pension. That is not what I desire. I think, there are so few people that would leave the country that the point has not been considered.
Could you in any way help me in this matter of getting the pension transferred?
Thanking you in anticipation, I am,
Yours truly,
W. T. Seagrief.
Perhaps the last part should be directed to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris). I would be happy to pass the appreciation back to the minister if he would make that possible. I feel there are many other ways, Mr. Speaker, in which our senior citizens could be provided with further assistance. I am not going to refer to them this afternoon
Private Bills
because they have been mentioned in previous debates, but certainly action with respect to these matters is long overdue. On behalf of those who exist in straitened economic circumstances I would request the sympathetic and the favourable consideration of the minister and of the government.
I am not a member of the estimates committee but I was interested to read an account in the paper of part of the sessions of the estimates committee in regard to old age pensions. The Globe and Mail of April 13, 1956, carried the following heading:
$40 Old Age Allowances Won't Be Increased. Martin Tells Commons.
The opening paragraph reads as follows:
Health Minister Martin made it clear today that the federal government has no intention of increasing the $40 a month old age pension. He said any further assistance for Canada's 1,217,000 citizens of pensionable age would have to come from the provinces, Ottawa has discharged its responsibility in full.
I am glad that statement is not in quotation marks, because I would not like to think that the Minister of National Health and Welfare made the statement that Ottawa has discharged its responsibility in full. I ask, how much longer are our senior citizens to be consigned to penury? How much longer are we to finance our economy with such lavish expenditures while leaving the builders of our nation to struggle on in poverty? Some of the provinces at least are doing what they can, and certainly the federal government should take some action and raise the old age pension allowances and make them payable anywhere the pensioners choose to spend their declining days, and* also give them consideration in other respects as well. Do you wish to call it five o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

Mr. Speaker, at this time I should like to say a few more words in an effort to persuade, if possible, the members of the house that Canada does not need another finance company. We feel that for reasons of consumer purchases there are already sufficient credit facilities available to the Canadian people. There are credit facilities available that are much more in line with the needs of the people than those facilities offered by the existing finance companies. Therefore we believe it is our responsibility not to lend a hand to foster the growth of Canadian finance companies.
In our efforts on this bill I was rather disappointed to find that few of those members who, rightly or wrongly, are regarded by many Canadian working people and farmers as being in sympathy with the welfare of the ordinary citizen have helped us in this

Private Bills
debate. Very often we read of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) expressing great concern for the well-being of the ordinary Canadian people. He did not see fit to rise in his place and put up a battle on behalf of the common people in order to protect them from another finance company.
The hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) and the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Philpott) also did not see fit to rise in their places and plead in the interests of the people in an effort to avoid another finance company being established. I can understand the position of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), who is often advertised as the kindly man of Canada. I can see that with the president of the Liberal federation interested in this particular measure the Prime Minister could not very well make a speech on behalf of the working people of Canada.
We are convinced, Mr. Speaker, that there is absolutely no need for this additional company to be organized. I am glad that there are at least two members on the Liberal side of the house who agree with us, and I should like to mention them again. The hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Goode) has once again shown his integrity when he feels that the people of his riding are vitally concerned in an issue. The hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Hollingworth) has also indicated that he is concerned about the welfare of the people who elected him to the high office that he now holds.
I think a great deal of credit is also due to the newspapers of Canada for their efforts to help us to make the Canadian people aware of the high interest rates they are paying, the evils that exist in the operations of finance companies and their recognition of the efforts we have made here. I note with some concern the absence of publicity given to this whole subject by the newspaper operated by the Southam Press. I am just wondering whether Mr. MacTavish, being a director of the Southam Press, might have something to do with the almost blacklisting of this subject matter by newspapers operated by that organization. In this morning's Globe and Mail I noticed a letter attacking the position I have taken in this house and pointing out how respectable finance companies are in their dealings with the people. On mentioning this letter to one hon. member I received this reply: Yes, the hangman always wears a nice uniform and is always very formal and very respectable. That is the attitude we take to these unnecessary organizations and we again intend to oppose the formation of another such organization.

This bill, Mr. Speaker, would incorporate in Canada another wholly-owned subsidiary of a United States company. If the discussion that has taken place in this house from time to time about the danger of United States capital on coming into Canada controlling industry and controlling various fields of endeavour in this country means anything at all, it means that this is precisely the kind of measure to which this house should give careful scrutiny. In the small loans field today the twc>
largest companies, both wholly-owned by parent United States companies, control 83 per cent of the field. The Conservative party have made reference, as have we, to the fact that certain industries in this country are gradually coming under the domination of United States capital. Various percentages have been pointed out to show the extent to which some industries have come under the control of United States capital. In the publication that was referred to earlier today in this house and the publication referred to by the Financial Post of April 14, two aspects of the petroleum picture are shown. With regard to exploration and development, United States control is 59 per cent; in refining, it is 71 per cent and in transportation, it is 100 per cent.

What I am saying is this. If the attitude that is being taken by many members in this house with regard to the need to look carefully at allowing United States capital to control further large segments of Canadian industry and Canadian business means anything, this is the type of bill and the type of company which every hon. member of this house who is in any way questioning the intrusion of United States capital into this country should vote against.
