speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. The hon. member must not anticipate the vote that will be given

on this measure. This measure is up for discussion now. The house has not yet voted on this measure. I do not see how he can analyse the attitude of hon. members before they have decided on it.

I think I can analyse it quite accurately from their own remarks recorded in the debate on this bill on Friday last as found at pages 2933 and 2934 of Hansard. At that time the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) and the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) made it perfectly clear that the position of the Conservative party was to support the passing of this bill and its referral to the banking and commerce committee. If one of the members of that party wishes to say that I am wrongly interpreting their position, I shall be most happy to correct that interpretation. But I feel that it is a correct interpretation on the basis of the statements of the hon. members themselves.
We in this group are opposed to this bill for a number of reasons. We are opposed to it for the reason given by the superintendent of insurance, Mr. MacGregor, namely that it would not be a service to ordinary Canadians and to potential borrowers to have another company incorporated and to see further companies participating in this field; that by an extension of the number of companies in this field, and with many small companies in the field, you will have inefficient companies operating and the battle to get lower interest rates will be made more difficult. We are further opposed to the passing of this bill because we believe that the huge interest rates that are being charged by small loans companies are wrong and that we should not, by supporting this measure, incorporate another company that will occupy this field and will charge such gigantic interest rates. I believe we should oppose this bill because the company is a wholly-owned subsidiary of a United States company and this field is already fully occupied, I believe that there is no reason why we should be giving approval to the passage of this bill.
I am amazed at the stand that has been taken by the Conservative party in connection with the passing of this bill. On looking over the bill itself I note that it is a bill to incorporate a company that will be wholly owned by a United States company, namely the Massachusetts Acceptance Corporation, and that two of the directors of the parent company are to act as directors of this company. In their battle against having United States capital come into this country and against having United States capital in the business of constructing and operating pipe lines, the Conservative party have been 67509-1914
Private Bills
extremely vocal. They have been very strong in their statements. The hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) in his speech in Saskatoon as recently as April 6 is reported in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix of Saturday, April 7, as saying that his party is opposed to Texas buccaneers coming into Canada to operate this particular project. The article reads in part as follows:
John Diefenbaker Thursday evening promised that "Texas buccaneers" would not get control of the natural gas outlet from western Canada. The M.P. for Prince Albert told a Saskatoon constituency nominating meeting that the Progressive Conservatives were preparing a fight in the House of Commons on the proposed trans-Canada pipe line that would make the recent filibuster on the Defence Production Act look like a mere skirmish.
If the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) is to be consistent, if the speech made this afternoon by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) means anything, surely it means that the Conservative party should be opposing the intrusion into Canada of Massachusetts marauders who are being incorporated by this bill just as strenuously as they are opposing United States capital coming in here and labelling it, as they do, Texas buccaneers. We in this group are being completely consistent in opposing this measure. We regret very much that' the support we have obtained has not been unanimous, and particularly has not been unanimous so far as all opposition members are concerned.
The hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings and the hon. member for Greenwood said that they were going to support the passing of this bill because by that means they would allow it to be referred to the banking and commerce committee for study. Since when does a member of parliament have to support the second reading of any bill merely to have the details of that bill discussed before a committee? I say we should state whether we are for or against the principle of the bill. If we are against the principle of the bill then we should not take into account at all whether we are going to have an opportunity of considering the details in a committee of this house. In order to be consistent we should, if we are opposed to the measure, vote against it on second reading.
The Conservative party used to do that. I can remember so well that on so many occasions the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) opposed the incorporation of certain pipeline companies. He was anxious that a Canadian route should be followed. In discussing these private bills for the incorporation of private companies the Conservative party did not say, we are going to have to vote for them on second reading in order to have a chance to discuss the details in a committee.

Private Bills
No, they said the bills were wrong and they did not want those companies incorporated, at least until they would agree to follow a Canadian route. Until that was done they were going to oppose them on second reading. They opposed them by proposing a six months' hoist and they used another weapon that is really more effective. They talked them out for a whole session and they killed at least one bill by that method. I suggest that instead of taking this wishy-washy attitude and saying they are going to have to vote for second reading in order to have a detailed discussion, they should be consistent. They should do as the Leader of the Opposition said they were going to do as a party; they should do as the hon. member for Prince Albert says they are going to do; they should do as the hon. member for Kamloops this afternoon said they were going to do, namely to protect the Canadian nation from this tremendous, overbearing intrusion of United States capital in the small loans field. The Conservative party is once again riding two horses with great ability, but the horses are going in opposite directions. They are able to stand up and say they will vote for the incorporation of another company with United States capital to occupy a field that is now dominated by United States companies. But when it comes to United States capital in the pipeline field, they are against it.
I suggest that the Conservative party should take another look at its attitude. If it wants to oppose the further encroachment of United States capital into various industries, even at this late time they should join with the C.C.F. group in opposing the passage of this measure. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we shall, when the opportunity arises, call for a recorded vote and shall vote in opposition to this measure.

was going to make a few observations about this bill, Mr. Speaker, but since the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) has been rather lengthy I shall make a very brief comment because I feel hon. members would like to vote on this measure this afternoon. Mr. Speaker, before leaving the subject with which I was dealing at five o'clock, I would just like to commend to the attention of the Minister of Finance a letter, a copy of which I have received-and I believe all other members from British Columbia have received it-from the old age pensioners' organization. It is signed by E. A. Griffin, provincial secretary. The copy I have is endorsed by John Campbell, president, and Mrs. Edith Wallace, secretary of the Mission City, B.C., branch. The letter states:
I have been directed by the board of directors of the British Columbia old age pensioners' organization to forward to you the accompanying facts and petition to ask that your honourable house take immediate steps to insure that all old age pensioners throughout the dominion receive sufficient income, adequate housing, home nursing care and nursing homes for those needing such accommodation and hospitals for chronic cases.
I have been asked to remind your honourable house that little has been done by the federal government since 1927 to improve the lot of the old age pensioners throughout the dominion and any increase in the federal old age pension since that date has only been secured as the result of pressure brought to bear on the federal government by the provinces.
Moreover the amount of such increase in the basic pension bears no relation whatever to the tremendous increase in the cost of living as compared to the cost of living in 1927.
I would like to call the attention of your honourable house to the fact that the age at which the basic pension of $40 per month is granted is the highest in the world. The age at which the old age pension is granted in other countries ranges from 50 years of age in Uruguay to 67 years in Iceland and Sweden.
We therefore humbly pray that your honourable house take immediate steps to raise the basic pension of $40 per month to $60 per month to be paid to women at 60 years of age and to men at 65 years of age.
We also ask that the Department of National Health and Welfare or such other authority as may be deemed necessary undertake the immediate survey of the housing needs of every locality throughout the dominion and adequate provision be made for low cost housing for old age pensioners, hospitals for chronic cases among old age pensioners, nursing homes for those needing such accommodation; also homes for the infirm where such attention as may be needed may be given.
3016	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Patterson
We also humbly pray that the taxable limit oi $60 per year for old age pension purposes be abolished and every income be taxed for this purpose on a pro rata basis.
I would like to place that on the record because it represents the views of the old age pensioners organization of British Columbia.
With respect to health and welfare programs, I also wish to support the request being made on behalf of our blind friends for a grant, free from the means test, to cover the cost of guiding services. I received a considerable number of requests that we give our support to this particular project. I am not going to take time to read them but I have a list here of at least 13 different institutes and organizations of various kinds in the province of British Columbia, most of them in my own riding. I feel that this is a worthy cause. It has been mentioned by different members in the house. I would ask that the matter receive the sympathetic consideration of the Minister of Finance.
There is another matter that I called to the attention of the minister last year. This has to do with deductions permitted for income tax purposes on contributions for charitable, educational and religious purposes. I indicated, I believe, last year, and I would just like to state again, that in the United States of America up to 20 per cent of the individual's gross income paid to charitable and religious organizations can be exempted from income tax when making returns.
I have also made some inquiries regarding the United Kingdom and find that there is there a system of covenanting, by which means a person is able to give the religious society the advantage of the income tax paid on the money. For example, the religious society reports these gifts, along with copies of the actual covenant forms signed by the donors, and then is able to reclaim the income tax paid by the individual to add to the society funds. In this particular instance, it is not the person himself who benefits from the income tax deductions for these purposes but the organization to which his contributions are made. As far as the Department of National Revenue would be concerned, there would not be any difference in this particular respect. I believe that increases in these deductions would be beneficial. It would give recognition to the work that such organizations are doing, as they are in a large sense providing the very foundation of our free democratic way of life. I believe it would encourage giving to these various purposes.
There are a considerable number of people in Canada who feel conscience bound to contribute at least ten per cent of their income to the church of their choice. Some, of course,


give more; some give less; and I suppose some do not give any. Nevertheless, some feel, as 1 have said, conscience bound to make that contribution of at least ten per cent to the church of their choice. In that case it does not allow for any contributions whatsoever to educational and to charitable organizations. I should like to emphasize that again. I thought the minister evidenced some slight interest in this matter last year when I called it to his attention. I should like to think it was an oversight rather than deliberate intent that explains the absence of any reference in the budget to increased allowable deductions in this respect.
There is one other matter I should like to deal with very briefly at this time. We have had considerable discussions, and no doubt we shall have further discussions, relative to the supposed United States domination of the Canadian economy through increased and constantly increasing investment. I am sure we have all read glowing reports of Canadian resources. We can turn to magazine or newspaper articles and we can listen to public speeches and find so many people referring constantly to the tremendous resources that are ours in Canada. Referring to the prospects for the future, these same writers and speakers paint in glowing terms the possibilities of future development in our great nation. We all realize, of course, that capital is required for these developments.

In the Toronto Globe and Mail of April 16, 1956 there was an article headed, "U.S. Students are Surprised by Antagonism", which reads in part as follows:
Biggest surprise to University of Rochester students is Canadian antagonism to Americans.
I am not going to read any more because my time is almost gone and I have one or two other things to say. I say that it seems as though there are a great many more who are joining in the chorus of anti-Americanism and I ask the question: What is behind it all? We hear a great deal about the development of the Soviet economy and the tremendous strides being made in that country, and it would appear that the attitude that so many are taking today would have the effect of sabotaging our own development in Canada. I do not think that is what we want at all. I do not believe it is what we desire.
Of course we prefer that Canada be developed by Canadians and by Canadian capital, but let me say again that the government consistently refuses to adopt policies whereby the nation's credit could be used for these purposes. Nevertheless, development there must be. We have had it pointed out that Canadians will not invest. The hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) referred to proceedings in the railway committee where it was learned that only $2 million out of $143 million was offered by Canadian insurance companies for the financing of a railroad construction project.
If Canadians will not invest, if the government will not act, then what is the alternative? I believe that continued development is both desirable and essential and, as I said, much as we prefer Canadian development of Canadian resources, if that is not possible and the government refuses to adopt policies that will encourage Canadian investment then
The Budget-Mr. Patterson I believe that we should be prepared to welcome foreign capital in Canada.
I should like to call attention to the Financial Post of March 17, 1956. Here on the front page of one of the sections of that paper we find the following under the heading "The Prancing Prosperity of Canada's West Coast":
A $220 million expansion program in the pulp and paper industry.

Government, with a new boldness of concept, is directing record capital outlays to push communication and transportation services into all parts of the country, to facilitate the big undertakings, bring a new degree of cohesion to the province and all that is taking place therein. Foreign investment capital, more aggressive now than at any time since end of world war II, has eager eyes on the fast developing British Columbia scene. That is under a Social Credit government. I should like to call attention to an article in the Montreal Gazette of Tuesday, April 17, 1956, headed "Foreign Money Welcome Here, Beaulieu Says". The article reads in part as follows:
"We have not enough venture capital in Canada to develop our resources. We welcome capital from abroad. It gives us employment which we would not otherwise have. Foreign capital, in fact, represents our livelihood", said Mr. Beaulieu.
He said foreign investment is becoming more diversified, both in its source and in the type of investment. "We used to get our foreign capital from the United States in the form of investment in our resources industries", he said. This indicates, Mr. Speaker, that we are receiving capital not only from the United States of America but from the European countries as well. Finally, I do not say that we should not consider the other side of the

The Budget-Mr. Decore picture. I do not say that Canadian industry and resources should be turned over to foreign interests.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I want to compliment the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) on having brought down for the benefit of the people of Canada a budget which is not only sound but realistic. I have listened with a great deal of interest to what has been said by the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Patterson) and I share his desire. I should like to see increases made in old age pensions and our other social security benefits. I should like to see a widening of our social security benefits. However, there is always a limiting factor and that factor is the ability to pay. There is no magic formula by means of which the money can be raised. In spite of all the fancy theories we hear as to how the money can be raised, we know that the money can only be raised by taxing the people of Canada and there is a limit to how far you can go in taxing the people.
I am sure that the minister would like to see a reduction in the taxes imposed at the present time if that were only possible. But let us not forget that this year, as we have in the last number of years, we are appropriating nearly $2 billion of our budget for national defence or, in other words, more than 40 cents out of every dollar raised through taxation from the people of Canada by the government goes for national defence. We must be realistic. In view of the international situation, we must take these steps in order to preserve peace. Once we feel that we can safely reduce our expenditures on national defence then, of course, we can very easily reduce taxes and at the same time widen the benefits in the social security field.
I am hopeful that the time will soon come when, without endangering our national security, it will be safe to reduce our expenditures on national defence and thereby to reduce taxes while at the same time increasing our social security benefits. I believe we have in this country one of the finest programs of social security in the world. That this government is social security minded is indicated by the fact that, apart from other social security measures, in 1948, a program of national health was commenced. Now the

federal government, in conjunction or cooperation with the provinces, is endeavouring to introduce a health insurance scheme.
At this time, Mr. Speaker, I should like to draw to the attention of this house and especially to the attention of the government a matter which I consider to be of great concern in the prairie provinces, especially Alberta, the province from which I come. I wish to make reference to the freight rate structure and to some of the recent manipulations of the railway companies which, in my opinion, have had an adverse effect on our Alberta economy. Hon. members will recall that in 1951 the royal commission on transportation known as the Turgeon commission, after sitting for some two years, came out with a 200,000-word report. This commission was concerned mainly in reporting on methods for equalizing freight rates in all parts of Canada. The reason that the government decided to have this commission appointed was mainly the complaints that were made from the maritime provinces and the prairie provinces. The prairie provinces and the maritime provinces felt that there was unfair and unjust discrimination with regard to freight rates. Among other things, the recommendation of this commission had the effect of creating a new deal in rail freight rates throughout Canada. There was wide equalization with the aid of a $7 million a year subsidy. It was felt that rarely if ever have complainants under confederation won so notable and justifiable a victory as did the prairie and maritime provinces under the Turgeon report. I feel that such a victory could hardly have been possible without the silent acquiescence of the two central provinces, namely Ontario and Quebec. They did not even appear before this commission or give evidence. If they had appeared before it they would have had to defend the recognized discrimination in their own favour. Hence this recommendation of the Turgeon commission was hailed in many quarters throughout Canada as a great step towards national unity.
We realize that the geography of this country provides an extremely difficult problem with regard to national transportation. It is difficult to overcome all the disadvantages or to eliminate all discrimination. The three prairie provinces in particular suffered a great deal because of their geographic position, their distance from markets, their distance from manufacturing centres and a small population. We in the three prairie provinces have hardly a self-sustaining population. Of the several complaints that were made by the prairie provinces before this commission made its report-especially by the

province of Alberta-the most bitter complaint was with regard to this old rate system. Under that old rate system it cost far more to ship many classes of goods to Edmonton or Calgary than it did to ship them an additional 600 miles through the extremely difficult terrain of the Rocky mountains to Vancouver. The railway companies gave special low rates to the Pacific coast ostensibly to meet water transport competition. It was felt that the particular loss of revenue which the railway company sustained had to be borne in large measure by the prairie provinces, because in the prairie provinces the railway companies had few agencies that were able to compete with them with regard to traffic. Hence the Turgeon recommendation endeavoured to do away with this abuse.
This commission recommended what was known as the one and one-third rule. Under this one and one-third rule the railway companies were forbidden to impose for shipments to Alberta a charge of more than one and one-third times the corresponding rate to the Pacific coast. This recommendation of the Turgeon commission was subsequently implemented by legislation in this parliament. In spite of this legislation and in spite of this recommendation by this commission it would appear that the railway companies were able to find a loophole in the legislation. They took the stand that the one and one-third rule applies only to general tariffs but does not apply to the so-called agreed charges. By agreed charges is meant special arrangements that are made with particular persons or groups. We now see that for some months the railway companies have been entering into agreements with eastern Canadian manufacturers whereby they allow special low rates to the Pacific coast. The result of this procedure is simply to by-pass the Turgeon commission recommendation which endeavoured to bring about this equalization of freight rates on a more equitable basis and once again we see this wide gap between the costs of shipment of certain goods to Vancouver and the costs of shipment to Alberta points.
I have here some figures that have been prepared by the Alberta Freight Bureau. Some of these give examples of how freight rates from the central provinces to Edmonton and to Vancouver compare. Of course these rates to Vancouver are all based on these agreed charges. Here are some of them. On pig iron, from Sault Ste. Marie to Vancouver, the cost is $21.80 per ton; to Edmonton the cost is $33.59 per ton. On paint and varnish ingredients, from Montreal to Vancouver the rate per hundredweight is $2.25; to Edmonton it is $3.35. On cast iron pipe, from Toronto to Vancouver the rate per hundredweight
17, 1956
The Budget-Mr. J. B. Hamilton is $1.10; to Edmonton it is $2.44 or more than twice as much. On wire rods, from Hamilton to Vancouver the rate under these agreed charges is $1.20 per hundredweight; to Edmonton it is $2.80 per hundredweight; sheet metal from Hamilton to Vancouver, $1.10 per hundredweight and to Edmonton $2.30 per hundredweight; steel bars from Hamilton to Vancouver $1.30 per hundredweight and to Edmonton $3.23 per hundredweight. This is nearly three times the rate to Vancouver and yet there is this additional 600 miles through difficult terrain, the Rocky mountains.
As the Edmonton Journal in its editorial of March 16 puts it, in part:
It will be seen that this new type of discrimination applies particularly to materials and semi-finished goods used in manufacturing. The effect is to hamper Alberta's developing industries in competition with those in eastern Canada, especially in their efforts to obtain access to the big British Columbia market. A.part from the injury to existing firms, there is no doubt that the freight rate situation has helped to discourage a number of concerns which had planned to establish new industries in Alberta.
My concern, as well as the concern of the people of Alberta, is how far this is going to go and how wide a gap is going to be opened up. The one and one-third rule which has been recommended by the Turgeon commission is now becoming meaningless by virtue of the position taken by the railway companies. We in Alberta feel that this is downright discrimination; it is both unfair and unjust. It is my submission, Mr. Speaker, that every consideration should be given to bringing the so-called agreed charges now established by the railways under the one and one-third rule.

speechtext:
This
afternoon, Mr. Speaker, I was approached by the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. White) who asked me how long I was going to speak tonight and I was reminded of my experience in the courts and the frustration of waiting for cases to be heard. I was thinking though, Mr. Speaker, if I might make a suggestion, that certainly we have all felt that the rules in connection with the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne and the budget address have been a great improvement over the rules in previous years. However, I am wondering if instead of allotting the number of speakers by parties it might not be an improvement if each party were allotted a specified amount of time and given the privilege of working out within that amount of time the number of speakers who desired to take part in the debate. I feel there are a great many of us who would be quite content to speak for 15 or 20 minutes

The Budget-Mr. J. B. Hamilton and in that way enable perhaps 15 or 20 more speakers to participate in this most important discussion.
I am not going to take very long tonight and there is a reason for that. I think you are all waiting to hear the first effort of the new member for Temiscouata (Mr. St. Laurent). Let me say that since I am not following him in the debate I will not be able to congratulate him on his effort, but I can say that I sympathize with him at this time because everybody has had to go through this ordeal at some time or other in his career. I should like to say as well that it would give me a great deal of pleasure tonight to make one of those speeches that are sure to catch the headlines. Like the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Patterson), if I could not stop all the money that is going to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) I should like to give it all away after it gets there. Unfortunately, it is not possible for me to say I should like to double all the social security features. I cannot talk tonight about planes for Israel, magazine taxes or United States investment, but I do believe I have something to say about a problem which exists at the grass roots level. It is one which is being studiously avoided by this house, and that is the problem facing municipalities in connection with their financing. You know, this comes as a surprise to me because if one looks at the parliamentary guide one finds so many members in this house who have had lengthy experience on municipal councils, but apparently when they get to this lofty position in the senior government they forget all about the problems that they left at home.
I think perhaps I should not use the expression "senior government" because that does not give a true picture of the spot these municipal councils occupy in our governmental setup. The members of these municipal councils, in their sphere, are just as capable and as well qualified to deal with those problems as we are to deal with ours. They face the same number of problems and just as great problems as we do here. However, to paraphrase Mark Twain I would say that everybody talks about the municipalities but nobody does anything about them. The hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Holling-worth) spoke to me just a few moments ago and said he was going to look after the interests of that particular part of the province. I am quite sure I can say to the hon. member tonight that anything I say about York West is equally applicable to his riding, and his problems there are just as important as ours. When I talk about these problems tonight I do not want to restrict myself in any way to the particular riding I represent 

because I feel if you do that in this debate you are abusing the privilege of taking part in it.
Municipal governments as we know them in this country, and perhaps particularly in Ontario, have reached the breaking point, yet the higher levels of government appear totally unconcerned. The chief occupation of the higher governments at the moment appears to be to hold conference after conference, issue statement after statement, but not to do anything while allowing the municipalities to continue sinking. The plain truth of the matter, Mr. Speaker, is that realty taxes cannot begin to cope with the demands made upon municipal treasuries. This is most important in connection with education costs. In an expanding economy in which it is called upon to provide increasing services the municipality, with its narrow tax base, simply cannot perform its proper functions. The responsibility for applying remedies lies with the senior levels of government, and when I say that I mean provincial governments as well as the federal government.
It is cold comfort for the municipal taxpayer, saddled as he is with these crippling taxes, to listen to his representatives in the provincial house or this house extend condolences and drip crocodile tears while doing nothing to ease the strain. The home owner has had to foot the bill just like a milch cow, and up to now he has been an uncomplaining animal who gives and gives because that is what he has always done.
The federal government brings in hundreds of thousands of newcomers to this country. We all agree that we need them; but immediately they step off the boat and immediately they get their first pay cheque this government takes a big bite for its own tax purposes. The federal treasury receives the revenue and the municipality gets the headaches. It is high time that all governments took a long look at the problem of education costs and divorced them entirely from real estate taxes. The cost of education should be redistributed on a more equitable basis in order to get the home owner off the hook. Buck-passing has become a fashionable pastime, Mr. Speaker, in this connection but the time may not be far off when an aroused public will demand more than talk. Municipal governments need help, and they need it desperately; but there seems little awareness of the gravity of the situation on the part of this government or of other senior levels of government. Municipal governments are the poor relatives trying to exist and provide for a family that grows and grows and whose wants become greater and greater. Unless there is help, the education system in

Ontario, Mr. Speaker, particularly in the metropolitan area of Toronto, faces a breakdown.
I am not going to quote from any lengthy articles or editorials, Mr. Speaker. I am sure that you have been subjected to enough quotations today. I saw a couple of articles just the other night in the Evening Telegram. One article was written by Arthur Spence and appeared in the Toronto Telegram entitled, "Fight About Schools". In the same paper there was an editorial entitled "Frills and Essentials". But, Mr. Speaker, it is boiling down to this. The provincial treasury does not have the money to pass on to the municipalities. It has had to provide some cuts in expenditures in order to carry on on an equalized basis from one municipality to the other. In order to do that, such items as domestic science classes, gymnasiums, manual training rooms, are now required to be dropped from school plans if there is to be any new school building in the area of greater Toronto. I leave it to you, Mr. Speaker, and to hon. members, to consider whether items such as these can be classified as frills. And yet, if the financial problem is left the way it is those types of facilities may be dropped from new school construction.
Is there an answer in increased realty taxes? I doubt it very much, sir. This problem exists all over, but I should like to illustrate it to you tonight to indicate to you the seriousness of the situation. I hold in my hand the New Toronto Advertiser, a paper with the largest weekly circulation in the province of Ontario. I should like you to look at these headlines. "Frustrate Tax-Control Bid". The following week this headline appeared "Fight 30 Per Cent Tax Hike". "Widow Urges Tax Strike, Many Consider Selling". If the people at this level are beginning to talk about tax strikes, then I think we should realize the situation. The following week this headline appeared: "Tax Prospects Frightening". The heading on the inside part of the paper is as follows: "Higher Long Branch Taxes Force Widow to Sell. Can't Pay Extra 10-Mill Boost to Improve Roads".
I do not know about the Minister of Finance, Mr. Speaker; I do not know whether he has all the money which he should have to meet all of the new types of requests that we are going to make if the suggestion of the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Patterson) is acceded to, but if the tax structure breaks down at the base, then the welfare payments are not going to be forthcoming at the top.
Our party has considered and has made recommendations at various times as to what
17. 1956
The Budget-Mr. J. B. Hamilton might be done in connection with this situation. As far back as 1952, in our amendment to the address in reply to the speech from the throne, the following words were included:
To reach agreement with the provincial governments in regard to clearly defined reallocation of taxing powers so that the provincial governments and municipal councils may have adequate financial resources to carry out their rapidly increasing responsibilities.
A clear measure of the responsibility and the necessity of help which is required by the municipalities. I am wondering whether any honest approach has really been made to this problem? Is it a continuation of this taxing authority saying to the provinces, "That is your responsibility", and the provinces saying, "We need more money from you in order to do the job."
I do not think I need to apologize in connection with this suggestion because I understand it was made by the premier of Manitoba. He said, in connection with the negotiations which took place here most recently between the provinces and the dominion, that around the conference table there should have been another chair for a representative of those municipalities. There is no use our saying that the municipal government is the creature of the province. There is only one dollar to be extracted from the taxpayer, and there will have to be a new method of dividing it.
A year ago in this chamber we discussed the question of changes in the Municipal Grants Act but I am sorry to say, Mr. Speaker, we did not get very far. The federal government thinks that apparently it is a pleasure for most municipalities to have federal buildings located in their districts, and that those districts should get down on their hands and knees and thank this government for being so kind. But I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that that type of construction requires the same services and requires all of the help from the municipality to maintain that any other type of construction requires. As a matter of fact, when we discussed this last year-and I think it is contained in the legislation passed in connection with the grants that were given-this government wanted to remove any assessment dealing with ornamental features on the building. I may say that the amount of money that we spend on some buildings approximates $22.50 a square foot and there must be an awful lot of ornamental features, when we talk about that amount.
I was talking to the president of one of our home and school associations, and as I walked into one of our school buildings I saw some marble walls and terrazzo floors. I said: "This looks a little nicer than when

The Budget-Mr. J. B. Hamilton I went' to school". The president of that association turned to me and said: "Mr. Hamilton, if all the public buildings in Canada can have marble entranceways and terrazzo floors and all the carved features, then surely it is not too good to provide the same thing for the students going into our institutions". Therefore, if we are talking about economy, if we are talking about removing the frills, then we should take into consideration the removal of some of the frills from some of our own activities. What might we do? What might be the solution of this problem? First of all, I think that this government should consider paying in full on a full assessment its share of the taxes wherever it has buildings in any municipality. It seems to me that that is only right, that that is a step in the right direction.
I think we have advocated before, and we should continue to advocate, the complete removal of sales and excise taxes on purchases by municipalities. I do not know how far you can carry this, I do not know how much you want the taxpayer to pay. I mean, it is his own material going into his own institution and yet you are asking him to pay two or three times before it gets into the bricks and mortar.
Then I submit we have to do one further thing as a temporary solution in an effort to broaden the tax base. We have had a lot of suggestions-I have made a couple myself on previous occasions-as to what we might do for the real property taxpayer. I can see some reason for burdening real estate with the costs of police and fire protection, garbage collection and the provision of various services, but I cannot see the necessity of burdening it with almost the total cost of education.
One way to broaden the tax base is to allow that part of real property taxation applicable to schools or school purposes as a deduction from federal income tax. Someone may well say that we would then have to increase the federal income tax. That might be true, but at the same time it would broaden the tax base and ensure that all of those who are subject to this particular type of tax are paying their fair share. As I look at the various activities of the government I am quite satisfied that if this course were taken the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) could probably make sufficient saving in his expenditures to provide that type of relief without additional taxes.
It may be said that this would be only a temporary solution, and that might be so, but there is a permanent solution. The federal government in co-operation with the provinces should take over the tax situation in connection with education. Someone will say that


that would be infringing on provincial rights, but this government never hesitates to move forward when it is something which politically suits its purpose. I am quite sure that it could do the job in this instance as well.
The things which I have said do not apply only to my particular area, although the problems there are great. I am sure that within the next year we will have 140,000 people living within the confines of York West. The burden of providing for institutions of education and similar facilities is becoming almost unbearable. When I refer to the problem of frills and essentials which are arising here, similar problems are arising in other ridings. I picked up a little pamphlet with reference to the election which is going to take place in Saskatchewan, I understand some time this year, and noted that they are considering the same things there. They talk of reduced taxes on property, the paying of 50 per cent of the local educational cost, the exempting of the municipalities from sales and excise taxes. I say to the Minister of Finance that these things do not apply to any particular area in Canada, they apply to Canada from one ocean to the other.
In conclusion-I understand you are not supposed to use that expression-it seems that everyone has said that there is nothing surprising about this budget. But in my very short tenure in this house I find something surprising about it. The Minister of Finance said that he hoped some of the optimism of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) would rub off on him. The surprising thing about this budget to me is the fact that it was brought in by the Minister of Finance when it might have been brought in by the Minister of Trade and Commerce because he does everything else around here.

In return for this mark of great confidence which they have shown me I promise to serve, as their member, with all the devotion of which I am capable.

Some time ago in this house, the hon. member for Quebec West said something about me. Having neither the ability nor the competence to discuss matters which may properly be classed as garbage, I am constrained, with deepest regret-and I apologize for it to the members of this house-to refrain from any comment regarding the speech of the hon. member.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today the red shadow of communism casts its grim light over humanity and even in the drama of party battle, political leaders- unless they are to betray the trust of the people-must talk and act with a new degree of maturity. It is just not good enough for any political leader of any party in any part of Canada to sit back and enjoy the luxury of condemning what Canada is doing to help fight communism in the North Atlantic alliance or in southeast Asia.
I am not a separatist and the people of Quebec are not separatists, even though we assert with persistence the rights which were guaranteed us under the constitution. The best proof that we in Quebec are not separatists is that since confederation the majority of the members of parliament elected from Quebec have almost always been on the government side, even when the great Conservative leader, Sir John Macdonald, was prime minister of this country, which means that they have almost continually been in agreement with the majority of the members elected throughout the country.
As a Canadian citizen living in Quebec, I believe it is my duty to condemn in this house any effort to create the impression throughout Canada that Quebec is not a loyal part of the Canadian confederation. I believe that all members of this house have a right, if not a duty, to take as active a part as they can to ensure the best possible government in Canada or in their own provinces.
One of the questions that is now being asked in my province is this: "Why do we sell western surplus grain at ridiculously low prices to communist countries rather than to Quebec livestock men?" The short answer is that Quebec livestock men can buy grain cheaper in Quebec than the price charged for any Canadian grain to any other country, communist or otherwise, and Quebec livestock men do not think it is ridiculously cheap. Canada is not giving any of her surplus grain to the communist countries, nor is she selling them any bargain-priced grain that she denies her own people. We are selling our wheat at good prices, thanks to the good sense of this government.
The Budget-Mr. J. P. St. Laurent
The people of my province have been asked about gifts to other countries. There have been no gifts to any countries, apart from the Colombo plan and the United Nations technical assistance, and a few very small amounts for relief of disasters in friendly countries, some of which have helped us when we had disasters.
Another question we are being asked is, "Why do we give half a billion dollars of our income tax money to Colombo?" It is even said that nearly half a billion dollars has been thrown away on the countries of southeast Asia. To the members of this House of Commons who have voted the Canadian contribution to the Colombo plan countries during the past half-dozen years, it is not necessary to say it was no half billion dollars. The total amount voted since the inception of the Colombo plan in 1951, up to 1956, is $127,900,000.
All members of this House of Commons have agreed, as have the Canadian people, that it is necessary that Canada should join with other fortunate nations of the free world to help create conditions in these southeast Asian countries so that communism will not get control of that area with its strategic supplies.
The blunt fact is this, that in southeast Asia today there is a battle for the hearts and minds of one-quarter of mankind. The kind of world we and our children will live in may well be determined by the events in southeast Asia. The fight for the control of the world is between the communist nations and the free world. Canada has sent her dollars out to this vital economic battleground. She has sent her scientists, her engineers, her technicians out there in one of the greatest crusades in history.
Today, Canada is helping to write one of the most glorious chapters in the history of man, and yet there are a few irresponsible critics who think that this does not matter to our people. Last Saturday, April 14, the editor of the French newspaper Le Devoir, Mr. Gerard Filion, who visited the areas benefiting from the Colombo plan, had this to say about this great humanitarian effort:
(Translation):
The Colombo plan is a joint assistance scheme of the commonwealth countries, to enable India, Ceylon and Pakistan to feed their undernourished men, women and children, who are exposed to every deficiency disease and to all epidemics that undermine the peoples of Asia.
Contrary to general opinion, Colombo plan funds are not used to provide foodstuffs but to pay for the necessary equipment which will enable Indians, Pakistanians and Cingalese to produce their own food. The Canadian contribution has been used to build an irrigation and power dam north of Calcutta, to purchase farm tractors and
3024	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. J. P. St. Laurent buses for public transportation in the province of Bombay. Each country tries to safeguard the identity of the achievements made possible by its contribution.
Altogether foreign assistance, either under the Colombo plan or under Mr. Truman's point four, has allowed India to reach the objective of her first five-year plan and to launch a second one. Of course, the objective of the first plan was a modest one: restore the Indian's diet to what it was in 1939. Now that diet amounted to 1,800 calories a day, whereas at least 2,700 calories a day are required to keep the human body in good health.
In India, 85 per cent of the population, i.e. about 300 million people, are undernourished. The everyday care is to keep body and soul together. When famine strikes in one area and public authorities lack the means or the time to send supplies, thousands of deaths occur each day. In our American cities, each morning the garbage collectors pick up the leftovers from our tables: in an Indian city struck with famine, the collectors pick up, each morning, the bodies of people who, during the night, died of starvation.
Only those who have seen India can realize to what depths of misery humanity can sink. The poorest among our poor are millionaires compared to the 60 million untouchables of India.

No true Canadian will forget or forgive the way communists in Canada tried to sabotage the Canadian war effort in the days before Russia was attacked. Well, attempts to weaken the efforts of the free nations are just as truly attempts to sabotage a great economic and social crusade against communism.
Today the hot hells of hydrogen bombs are just 26 minutes away from places like Quebec city. Today human life is probably less secure collectively than at any time in history. Today, as never before, we need clear vision and a firm will if we are to avert the dangers that threaten us.
So today, as a very junior member of this house, and as a father who loves his children,
I express the hope that all Canadians in Quebec, and in other provinces as well, measure up to the challenge of these times. In these days, when human life is probably less secure than at any time in history, surely we can all unite to support Canada's sincere efforts to build up the united strength of a free world so that it can be strong to defend itself against communism.

I believe that, so far, my constituency has been the only one where two prime ministers of Canada, Sir John Macdonald, and the present Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), have had their summer residence. The former premier of Quebec, the Hon. L. A. Taschereau, also used to spend the summer months there.


The Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe and the Hon. Adelard Godbout were born in Temiscouata. Thus Temiscouata is well known for its prominent men, but, unfortunately, it is not so well known to Canadian industrialists.
This is why, Mr. Speaker, many business men of my riding supported my campaign last fall, outside of any political considerations, hoping that I might be able to interest some of my business friends to visit our area, and perhaps convince them to settle there. During my campaign, I promised the voters- and it was the only promise I made to them- that I would do my utmost to have industrialists visit my riding, in the hope that they might see the advantages of settling there: a large, experienced and orderly labour force; an excellent geographical location; a link between Canada and the United States, and between upper and lower Quebec; transport facilities by sea, by land and before long, I hope, by air.
Possibly the Temiscouata electors were not entirely wrong in giving me their support, for I am happy to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that, starting in 1956, our county will share in the economic development about which the minister waxed eloquent in his budget speech of March 20 last, inasmuch as an industry which will employ between 250 to 300 people within two years is about to start operating in my county any day now.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take this opportunity to congratulate the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. St. Laurent) on his maiden speech. I should also like to state that I envy him his ability to speak in both official languages. I should really like very much indeed to be able to address the house in both languages with the facility that he possesses. Unfortunately, sir, I cannot repeat these congratulations with respect to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) on his recent effort in the budget debate. In sitting back here and watching various members get up to speak in the budget debate it seems to me that we have a strange situation. Every government member seems to feel that he has to commence his speech by congratulating the Minister of Finance on a wonderful effort. I cannot quite agree with that. To me it seems to be praise that is falsely placed.
Last year, as I recall, various government speakers congratulated the Minister of

Finance on the fact that he was able to provide tax reductions. This year they seem to find room for praise in the simple fact that he did not provide any tax reductions. To me the budget is simply an unimaginative budget. It is a political budget. There is no doubt that the Minister of Finance might well have made some tax reductions this year but has seen fit to save them until some future time.
I should like to make a few remarks about my own riding. First of all, I should like to mention the plight of Ontario farmers. That has been referred to several times this session but I would repeat that I think the government should give grave consideration to remedies for the situation with which the farmer is faced. Any industry as basic as agriculture whose net income decreased 28 per cent in the period from 1951 to 1953 and a further 12 per cent in 1954 requires a great deal of consideration. This decrease, of course, has been suffered in a period when all other income has been undergoing a great growth.
When the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) spoke in the debate a few days ago he dealt with this problem in great detail. I do not propose to go into the detail that he did but I would suggest that the government give close study to his remarks. I believe they require a great deal of study. On this subject I would recommend, however, that the importation of skim milk powder and cheese be allowed only on such a basis as will guarantee our producers a fair return.
I have another matter affecting my riding that has to do with C.N.R. pensions. As we all know, the C.N.R. employees have at times suffered lay-offs. These employees while suffering a lay-off are always subject to recall and if they do not respond they lose their job seniority and all other privileges. This means they cannot improve their pension position during the period of a lay-off because of course any jobs they may take have to be of a temporary nature. They cannot withdraw their pension except on complete severance from employment. These employees have a complaint and in that regard I should like to refer to page 25 of the official text of the Canadian National Railways pension plan. I should like to read clause 201 (d) which defines "allowable service" as follows:
"Allowable service" means (i) service prior to July 1, 1942, computed and converted into months of service in accordance with the company's regulations pertaining thereto; (ii) service on or after July 1,	1942, on the basis that one month's
service shall be allowed for any month during which any service has been rendered to the company in respect of which salary or wages have been paid; and (iii) such other service as may be recognized under these rules or as may be specially authorized by the directors hereafter, converted into months of service.
The Budget-Mr. Monteith
In conjunction with that I should like to read the applicable part of clause 205 which is found on page 27 of the same booklet. That part reads as follows:
205. (1) Every member who entered the service before attaining age forty-five and who remains in the service until normal retirement date under these rules shall be granted a pension, payable monthly, the annual amount of which shall be his average annual salary or wages for the five or the ten years of his allowable service next preceding retirement, whichever is the larger, multiplied by the following percentages:
One per cent for each year of allowable service up to 20 years.
One and one-quarter per cent for each year of allowable service during the next ten years;
One and a half per cent for each year of allowable service over 30 years.
Twelve months of service computed as mentioned in clause (d) of rule 201 shall constitute a year of allowable service, and part of a year shall be computed proportionately.
It is my understanding, Mr. Speaker, that if an employee is laid off in that last five or ten years, after having had many years' service, it can well mean a reduction in the percentage applied to average salary or wages to arrive at his pension. I understand the employees would like the opportunity of personally making up their contributions to the trust fund during any period of lay-off. This request does not seem at all unreasonable to me, particularly as during any lay-off period the employees are handicapped in securing other employment. I would simply suggest that the Minister of Transport look into this matter and advise correction of any injustice there may be.
I should like to return to the budget for just a moment. The Minister of Finance said that he was proposing to make deductible for tax purposes the expenses of professional people and others incurred in attending two conventions annually in Canada. I cannot agree that this is reasonable. I do not see any reason why one of these conventions at least should not be outside of Canada. I am simply going to take the case of a doctor, and I am assuming that this legislation is probably being brought forward as the result of a tax appeal board case some few months ago. I am thinking of a doctor who, for instance, goes to New York to attend a convention. I have known such instances where doctors have gone to conventions there and have attended study classes eight hours a day for a whole week. They may have gone to a musical comedy at night. I do not doubt that they did, but I do not think they have tried to charge those expenses.
However, I feel that when the doctor comes back to Canada he is in a position to earn more income on which he is going to pay taxes. On top of that, I think he is much better prepared to look after the illnesses
3026	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Monteith of Canadian citizens. It only seems reasonable to me that he should at least be allowed one convention in the United States. The minister's proposal definitely stipulates two conventions annually in Canada. I suggest that the minister give that matter consideration.
Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, I understand from an answer by the Minister of Finance on the orders of the day today that income tax amendments are going to be brought down shortly. I may have more to say about income tax at that time, but at this moment I should like to mention the proposed magazine tax. I think it should not be considered at this time. It is discriminatory. If these magazines should add to their advertising rates the 20 per cent tax that has been suggested I see no reason why advertisers would not in turn reduce their advertising budgets or have less money left to spend on strictly Canadian magazines. It seems very logical to me.
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, I do not believe in trying to legislate as to what people should read except that I too believe that some of the trash on our newsstands should be done away with. This tax appears to me to be a special tax on a special group. It is a special form of government interference in the magazine business. Mr. Speaker, I recall that during my first session, or at any rate during my first period in the house during which there was a budget debate, the spring of 1954, Hon. Douglas Abbott, when he was minister of finance, proposed a tax on farm mutual fire insurance companies. Before the debate was concluded he saw fit to reverse his opinion on that matter and withdraw the proposal. I am suggesting to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) that it is not too late to withdraw this proposal of the suggested 20 per cent tax on advertising in certain magazines, which might well be the forerunner of a tax on free speech.
I just wish to say a word about direct investment in Canada by foreign capital. To use the words used in Vancouver yesterday I believe this has been "definitely beneficial rather than detrimental" to Canada. Is it not time, however, to consider ways and means of providing for greater participation by Canadians in the expanding economy of our country? Let me point out that we have no capital gains tax in Canada whereas there is such a tax in the United States. I think this is quite an encouragement in itself to United States capital investment in Canada. The Security Analysts Association of Toronto presented a brief to the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects. They point out that section 106 of the Income Tax Act appears to be the crux of the matter. I would also mention, of course, that the reciprocal


tax convention of 1951 enters into the situation. Those two matters, section 106 of the Income Tax Act and the reciprocal tax convention of 1951, amply illustrate that if a foreign corporation operates a subsidiary and allows no Canadian shareholders, the withholding tax on dividends going out of Canada is 5 per cent. If it permits less than 5 per cent ownership by Canadians, the withholding tax is still 5 per cent. If it permits more than 5 per cent participation by Canadians, the withholding tax jumps to 15 per cent. That simply means that the withholding tax is three times as great if more than 5 per cent of the ownership is Canadian.
I should like to review briefly the four types of companies to which I am going to refer. I could give examples actually of these types of companies but I do not think that is necessary. First there is type 1. This type of company has been founded as a branch of a foreign corporation. There is no Canadian interest. Canadians can invest only by buying shares of the parent foreign corporation. They would then have only a small interest in the Canadian operations as compared with the over-all operations. Dividends to Canadians from holdings of the parent company would suffer withholding tax by the foreign country. Canadians would also lose the 20 per cent credit for tax purposes on these dividends from foreign holdings. To me, Mr. Speaker, this is not altogether an attractive proposition.
Then there is type 2. These are companies in which Canadians held minority interest and have been bought up by foreign parent corporations. This to me seems like the wrong trend. It has the effect of reducing former joint undertakings to the stature of branch plants. The tax situation is the same as that in type I.
Then there is type 3: These companies were at one time largely Canadian owned companies and were bought out by foreign interests. The tax situation in this type 3 is the same as that in type 1 after this move has been taken. There is not any new industry but the tax laws have encouraged this move.
Type 4: Companies whose voting stock is owned by foreign interests but whose senior financing is done in Canada. If senior financing takes the form of debentures or bonds the interest on such is deductible from company earnings for tax purposes. Income from such interest to Canadian holders is not subject to the 20 per cent dividend credit. Actually the dividend tax situation is the same. The withholding tax situation is the same as that in the other types.
I understand a brief has been presented to the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects, the so-called Gordon commission, pointing out that there are certain

foreign corporations carrying on their entire business in Canada whose profits are taxed in a manner similarly to that in which the profits of Canadian companies are taxed but there was no withholding tax on the movement of profits out of Canada. I should like to point out that I welcome foreign investment in Canada but that there appear to be certain inequities. I would suggest a full review of the withholding tax structure in order to determine the volume of Canadian investment in Canadian corporations. I would hope that this review would result in ownership securities being available to Canadian investors. Instead of the withholding tax becoming lower as Canadian investment decreases, it might well be the other way. The present withholding tax structure encourages more and more foreign domination. From a straight dollar point of view the present withholding tax structure discourages United States corporations from permitting Canadian participation and our national revenue department receives only one-third of what it might receive on dividends going out of Canada. I suggest that a real study should be made of the problem as the tax structure may not be the only angle to be taken into consideration.
I should like to bring to the attention of the house the situation with regard to Aluminium Limited. The Canadian shares were purchased by the United States parent company and were issued to United States shareholders. Eventually some of these shares were in turn purchased by Canadians and Canadian interests now hold some $300 million of the equity stock of this company. It seems to me that a worthy thought might develop if a study is really made of the whole situation.
I have made some calculations here. They are based on the figures taken out of this booklet entitled "Canada's International Investment Position, 1926-1954" and issued by the dominion bureau of statistics. I should like to point out that at page 75 of this book the direct investment of the United States in Canada is given-that means investment in equity holdings; it does not mean in government bonds or that sort of thing-as $5,740 million. At page 73 the direct investment of Canada in the United States is given as $1,256 million. I am reducing that $1,256 million by approximately one-third as at page 50 of this book it is stated that the equity of Canadian residents in the direct investment abroad at the end of 1954 was less than two-thirds of the total investment from Canada. I am taking the United States position but it is less than two-thirds of the total investment from Canada. In other words, some of these Canadian holdings

The Budget-Mr. A. W. A. White abroad are in turn owned by foreign investors. As a result there is estimated to be one-third off total holdings of Canadian investment to arrive at the net Canadian picture abroad. So reducing the $1,256 million by $416 million in round figures we come to a net investment by Canadians in the United States of $840 million. I am going to deduct that $840 million from the figure of $5,740 million mentioned previously as United States direct investment in Canada. This gives you a net figure of excess investment by the United States in Canada of $4,900 million. I am presuming that there is probably a 5 per cent dividend paid on this $4,900 million which would equal $245 million; that is a dividend paid on this excess $4,900 million invested in Canada. A 15 per cent withholding tax on that would amount to $36,750,000. A 5 per cent withholding tax would amount to $12,250,000. In other words, as between a 5 per cent withholding tax and a 15 per cent withholding tax there is a difference of $24,500,000. I simply present these figures, Mr. Speaker, to indicate that we may be losing out on some tax revenues as well as discouraging the participation of Canadian industry. Incidentally, this $24,500,000 approximately equals our donation to the Colombo plan-at least up until this year.
In closing, sir, I would repeat that foreign capital investment in Canada's future has been definitely beneficial rather than detrimental. But let us examine the situation as it exists today quite closely. Surely, it is time we took a look at this picture. I know that time is running short and there is a member on the government side who would like to say a few words. I understand that actually he is supposed to be making a Tory speech. I hope that in the very few moments left he does not change his mind and vote for the government.

speakeroldname: Mr. A. W. A. White (Waterloo South):
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In
rising to take part in this debate, Mr. Speaker, I would first like to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) on the very able and realistic manner in which he has handled his department. The year 1955 was undoubtedly one of Canada's most prosperous years, and in my mind there is no doubt that the tax adjustments made by the minister last year, the effect of many of which will not be felt until this year, were responsible in no small way for the economic recovery that took place in this country. However, in spite of this great national prosperity there were some sectors of industry and agriculture which did not fully share in that prosperity. If Canada is going to maintain its present level of prosperity, then this increased business activity must accrue to the benefit of all sectors of the economy or else those sectors
3028	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. A. W. A. White which did not share in it must be assisted by government intervention.
It was for that reason I had no hesitation in supporting government legislation introduced at this session to assist western wheat farmers. It is also for that reason that I congratulate the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and the government on maintaining and continuing floor prices on butter, which I feel have helped the Canadian dairy industry. I should, however, like to draw to the attention of all hon. members of this house, and particularly the Minister of Finance, the depressed condition of the wool cloth industry in Canada. It is one of those industries in which I believe government intervention is not only necessary but justifiable.
The wool cloth industry is one of the oldest industries in this country and a large number of factories are located in small towns and villages where they are the main source of employment. A good example of this is Dominion Woollens and Worsteds plant in Hespeler, a town of approximately 3,600. Up until the year 1950 this factory employed over 1,300 persons, whereas today there are only 552 people employed and some of them are on short time. Between the years 1949 and 1950 employment in the Canadian wool cloth industry dropped from 10,500 to 6,000, a reduction of 43 per cent, and 17 factories closed their doors. Between 1954 and the present time five more textile mills, two of which were wool cloth factories, have ceased operations. The chief factor which seems to be slowly but surely eliminating the wool cloth industry in Canada is competition with imported fabrics from the United Kingdom where wage rates are substantially lower than in Canada.
There may be some who have the idea that the Canadian wool cloth industry is over-expanded and inefficient. In answer to that let me say that between the period 1945 and 1949, with full employment, the Canadian wool cloth industry was only able to supply 68 per cent of the domestic market. In the postwar years the industry spent over $35 million in plant and equipment. A recent survey indicates that there is a greater percentage of automatic equipment in use by the industry in this country than there is in the United Kingdom, so the industry is modernized and efficient. According to the latest information available the Canadian wool cloth industry is paying 2J times the wages that are paid in the United Kingdom. Since the cost of raw material is basically the same in both countries, as it is controlled


by world prices, and since Canada has a higher productivity now through the use of a greater percentage of automatic equipment, we are forced to the conclusion that the wide differential in wages is the major factor contributing to the loss of the domestic market by the Canadian wool cloth industry to British imports. There does not seem to be any immediate likelihood of narrowing the gap in the wages paid unless the value of the pound improves in relation to the Canadian dollar, and the possibility of that happening is very remote because England deliberately devalued her currency to gain access to world markets.
One must, therefore, look to some other solution to the difficulties that are besetting the Canadian wool cloth industry. In May 1954 Mr. Abbott, the then minister of finance, as a result of numerous representations made by the Canadian wool cloth industry, directed the tariff board to make a study of all relevant information concerning the Canadian wool cloth industry. He particularly directed them to examine tariff item 554b, with particular reference to the maximum under that item. I should now like to give to the house an outline of the background of tariff item 554b, which undoubtedly is one factor which has enabled the United Kingdom to take over the wool cloth market in Canada.
In the year 1935 there appeared for the first time a maximum British preferential duty on wool cloth coming into Canada. The particular tariff item provided for an ad valorem duty of 27J per cent and a specific duty of 17 cents per pound, with the proviso that the sum total of these two duties was not to exceed 65 cents a pound. The establishment of British preferential maximum duty of 65 cent's per pound was the result of a recommendation of the tariff board, based on its findings that cloths, both woollens and worsteds, selling in England at a price of $2 or more per pound, were not within the range of economical manufacture in Canada. In other words, the tariff board recommended that a ceiling be placed on the duty for high-priced specialty fabrics such as those used by custom tailors, and in this way restricted Canadian production to a range of cloth in which it was most efficient.
Raw materials and conversion costs were much lower in 1935 than they are today, and the average price of imported fabrics was only $1.02 a pound. Therefore, it can be readily seen that the maximum duty applied to only a very limited and special range of cloths.
This tariff item was revised in 1937 and again in 1948, and the duties were reduced

from 27J per cent to 20 per cent ad valorem. The specific duty was reduced from 17 cents to 12 cents per pound and the maximum was reduced to 50 cents per pound. The conversion costs of raw materials were much lower in 1935 than they are today.

The following answers, deposited with the Clerk of the house, are printed in the official report of debates pursuant to standing order 39:

1.	Has consideration been given by the government or the Canadian National Railways to making the pensions of retired male Canadian National Railways employees covered by the Intercolonial and Prince Edward Island railways employees' provident fund act applicable to their widows?
2.	If so, what decision has been arrived at?
3.	If not, will the matter be studied and reported upon?
Answer by:	Mr. Langlois, Parliamentary
Assistant, for the Minister of Transport:
Consideration has been given, and action has been taken to accord contributors to the Intercolonial and Prince Edward Island railways employees' provident fund the opportunity to transfer to the Canadian National Railways' pension plan and thus place themselves in the same position with respect to pensions and survivor benefits as other Canadian National Railways employees, but no such action has been taken with respect to pensions of retired male employees of the Canadian National Railways covered by the provident fund.

Question No. 324-Mr. Van Horne:
What action, if any, has been taken by the government to provide handicap allowances, without a means test, for our blind people?
Answer by: Hon. Paul Marlin (Minister of
National Health and Welfare):
Since January 1, 1952, blind persons over the age of 70 years have been entitled to receive federal pensions under the Old Age Security Act without a means test. As of that date persons over the age of 70 years receiving pensions in respect of blindness under the Old Age Pensions Act were transferred to the administration of the Old Age Security Act. Other blind persons over the age of 70 who were not eligible to receive pensions in respect of blindness under the Old Age Pensions Act on account of the means test in that act could qualify for pensions under the Old Age Security Act by making application to the proper federal authorities.
The Blind Persons Act provides for the payment of allowances, subject to a means test, to persons who have attained the age of 18 years. Since the Blind Persons Act came into force on January 1, 1952, the maximum amounts of income allowed have been increased from $840 a year to $960 a year in the case of an unmarried person and from $1,320 a year to $1,560 a year in the case of a married person. Where both spouses are blind the amount has been increased from $1,440 a year to $1,680 a year.
When provision was first made for pensions in respect of blindness by an amendment to the Old Age Pensions Act in 1937, the maximum income allowed in the case of an unmarried person was $440 a year and in the case of a married person, $640 a year. These amounts were increased in 1944 to $500 and $700 a year. By amendments to the Old Age Pensions Act in 1947 the maximum amounts of income were again increased to $720 in the case of an unmarried blind person, $1,200 in the case of a married blind person with a sighted spouse and $1,320 in the case of a married blind person with a blind spouse. As explained above these amounts were increased by the Blind Persons Act to $840 a year in the case of an unmarried person, to $1,320 a year in the case of a married blind person with a sighted spouse and to $1,440 a year in the case of a married blind person with a blind spouse. The various increases in the maximum amounts of income allowed have had the effect of relaxing the means test very considerably over the years since blind pensions were first established in 1937. speechtext:
1.	Did Trans-Canada Air Lines request the Manitoba liquor inquiry commission for approval of the serving of liquor by the glass on scheduled passenger flights?
2.	If not, did Trans-Canada Air Lines make such a request to some other body which in turn placed it before the said Manitoba liquor inquiry commission?
3.	On whose responsibility was such a request made?
4.	Was the making of such request in line with government policy?
Answer by: Mr. Dickey, Parliamentary Assistant, for the Minister of Trade and Commerce:
1.	Yes.
2.	Answered by No. 1.
3.	The management of Trans-Canada Air Lines.
4.	No question of government policy is involved as the request was made by the company on the advice of counsel who were of the opinion that such a request should be made to avoid the possibility that the company might be debarred indefinitely from serving alcoholic beverages.

1.	How many employees of the Canadian National Railways have been laid off since January 1, 1955, in the province of Newfoundland?
2.	For what reason?
3.	What was the length of service in each case?
4.	How long a period of employment has each to work until retirement with pension would have occurred?
Answer by: Mr. Langlois, Parliamentary
Assistant, for the Minister of Transport:
The management of the Canadian National Railways advise as follows:
1, 2, 3 and 4. Seasonal employment and resultant lay-offs at termination of seasonal programs have a substantial effect on figures relating to the strength of working forces, and the assembling of information as to layoffs would necessitate the assignment of special staff to examine numerous staff records. It is not ascertainable if employees have had their employment permanently severed, because there are employees on seniority lists who are recallable as required. Such employees may also exercise their seniority to take positions on other parts of the system to the extent the labour agreements permit. Lay-offs, when made, are strictly in accordance with the seniority principles prescribed in the agreements with the various employees' organizations.
The average level of employment in the Newfoundland district for the month of January, 1955, was 4568, whereas the average level in February, 1956, was 4916, the latter being the latest figure available.
Eligibility for pension under the Canadian National Railways pension rules depends on the attainment of a certain age and the accumulation of a certain number of years of service.
